events.title: Google Maps has renamed Lake Ontario 'Lake America' for Americans
events.summary: Google Maps said it changed the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" after the US Geographic Names Information System, the federal government's official database of place names, did the same. Bloomberg/Getty Images Google Maps now shows "Lake America" to US users after Trump ordered the name change. Canadian users will still see "Lake Ontario," while others will see both names. MapQuest went viral for refusing to change the name, while Apple Maps still says "Lake Ontario." Google Maps has made the switch — for Americans, at least. A search on the mapping app on Sunday shows the name "Lake America" for the body of water adjoining northern New York and southern Ontario, known until very recently — and still to most — as Lake Ontario. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday that he said would "immediately" rename the body of water to "Lake America." Canadian officials have said they will not recognize the new name. In a blog post, Google said it changed the lake's name after the US Geographic Names Information System, the federal government's official database of place names, did the same. "Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the U.S., people using Maps in the U.S. will see 'Lake America,'" the company said. Canadian users will still see "Lake Ontario," according to Google. Viewers in the rest of the world will see both names. As of Sunday, Apple Maps still says "Lake Ontario." The company did not respond to a request for comment sent on Sunday. Trump made the switch in retaliation after trade talks between the longtime allies broke down last week. The Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariffs on many Canadian goods on August 22. Canada then responded in kind. Trump is now threatening 50% tariffs on auto and steel imports from Canada. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said in an interview with ABC News on Sunday that those tariffs would be "devastating on the US." "A tariff on Canada is nothing more than a tax on the American people," he said. Many Google Maps users wondered if the company would follow Trump's lead after the president announced the change. MapQuest, the original online mapping service that Google obliterated despite having a near 10-year head start, briefly returned to prominence last week by refusing to change the name of the Great Lake. "We're not changing it," the company said in one post. In another, the company invited users to name the lake "whatever you want." The stalwart "we're not changing it" post has more than 5 million views on X. None of the account's 24 posts in July got more than two likes. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister who bowed out of trade negotiations after he said the United States introduced "unfair" last-minute changes, wrote in a post on X that "naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario." "The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari'io, which, appropriately, means 'the lake is beautiful, the lake is big'," Carney said. Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" shortly after returning to office, part of an effort to restore what he called names that honor "American greatness." Google, owing to its policy of following GNIS designations , also now refers to the body of water as the "Gulf of America" on Google Maps. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Recruiter places ‘phoenix’ firm into liquidation just months after repurchase erased millions in debt
events.summary: New company reportedly quickly fell behind with promised repayments to administrator A recruitment executive who was allowed to buy back the assets of his bust company in instalments, despite it accumulating almost £3m of debt, has placed his new business into liquidation after falling behind with promised payments to the administrator. The news is the latest event to raise questions about the practice of “ phoenixism ”, accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts. The tactic, which is legal, is often justified by supporters who argue it can save jobs and help secure some returns for creditors – although HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) estimates it costs the UK taxpayer hundreds of millions of pounds a year. Premier Group Recruitment went into administration in September 2025 owing £2.9m , including £647,000 to HMRC, which had begun enforcement proceedings against the company. The recruiter’s assets were acquired three days later by a new company, PGGBR Ltd, founded by Andrew Woosnam, Premier’s 99% shareholder, who made an initial £10,000 payment and promised to transfer a further £600,000 via monthly £25,000 instalments over the following two years. Despite a seemingly positive start for the new business – which offered its consultants an “all expenses paid” trip to Las Vegas for hitting their targets – the company quickly fell behind with its promised repayments, causing the administrators to file an update on its struggles with Companies House in March. On Sunday, filings at Companies House said PGGBR had appointed a voluntary liquidator . Woosnam, who had received a £1.2m director’s loan from the defunct Premier and had taken dividends out of the company totalling almost £2m since 2022, is also understood to have made a series of redundancies at the new business in July that industry sources said equated to at least half his staff. The company’s website, which now appears to have been taken down, listed a management team of 12 people. Sources with knowledge of the job losses also suggested that those affected had not been paid and that Woosnam was planning to launch another new company to take his recruitment business forward. Companies House records show that in June the businessman changed the name of a business he founded a year ago from PGUSA to PGREC. The problems at Premier chime with long-running questions concerning the efficacy of allowing connected parties to buy back their bust businesses by promising future payments – deferred considerations, in the industry jargon. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Research has suggested that poorer outcomes tend to occur in insolvencies where the assets are acquired by connected parties paying via future instalments. For example, research by the University of Wolverhampton, for the UK government’s 2014 Graham review , concluded: “The failure rate of a connected party sale increases from 15% of all cases without deferred consideration to 37% when deferred consideration is introduced. Generally, when deferred consideration is present, whether or not a connected sale is also present, the failure rate rises considerably.” Similar results were published by a 2018 study funded by the EU. It concluded: “When the sale was to connected purchasers, there was a significantly higher risk of buyer mortality.” Woosnam has been approached for comment.

events.title: Sony accuses Anthropic of 'brazen campaign' to train Claude on its music — and wants up to $150,000 a song
events.summary: Sony Music and Warner Chappell filed a lawsuit against Anthropic on Friday. Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Claude seems to be a music fan. Sony Music and Warner Chappell sued Anthropic on Friday. The music companies said Anthropic trained its Claude AI models on stolen, copyrighted works. Sony Music and Warner Chappell want Anthropic to pay up. The publishing companies filed a lawsuit against Anthropic in a Northern California district court on Friday. Anthropic cofounders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann were also named in the filing. "Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic's 'Claude' series of artificial intelligence ('AI') models," the companies said in the complaint. Anthropic denied the accusations in a statement. "We disagree with the publishers' claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court," the company said. Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell Music said Anthropic collected "thousands upon thousands" of copyrighted songs, including 80s anthem "Eye of the Tiger," Marvin Gaye's "Ain't No Mountain High Enough," Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas is You," and Taylor Swift's "Paper Rings." In the lawsuit, the publishing companies said Anthropic has pirated their copyrighted works through a range of methods, including two digital archives, Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror. In June 2025, a judge ruled that Anthropic downloaded over 7 million pirated books to train Claude. "Among the many millions of books that Defendants torrented from these illegal pirate websites were books containing the lyrics and sheet music to hundreds or more of Music Publishers' copyrighted musical compositions, identified in Exhibit A. Those works include 'Livin' On a Prayer,' 'September,' 'Great Balls of Fire,' 'Ramblin' Man,' and 'Hallelujah,'" the lawsuit says. As a result, Claude models generate identical or near-identical copies of the copyrighted work in their responses to users, the companies alleged. In the lawsuit, the companies said training Claude on copyrighted content allows it to produce AI-generated lyrics that will ultimately compete with human-made songs. Sony Music and Warner Chappell requested a jury trial. They're seeking statutory damages from Anthropic, including up to $150,000 for each composition it used to train Claude. "Even the most revolutionary of technologies must develop within the bounds of the law, and Anthropic's Claude models are no different," the companies said in the complaint. The AI industry has been targeted by a slew of copyright lawsuits since large language models like Claude and ChatGPT began to transform society. Tech companies need troves of data to train their AI models, and go to great lengths to acquire it. Most recently, historians and archivists have accused AI companies of acquiring large numbers of antique books and feeding them into their LLMs, destroying them in the process. Last September, Anthropic agreed to pay over $1.5 billion to authors to settle a class-action lawsuit related to pirated works. OpenAI, too, has faced several copyright lawsuits in recent years, including one from The New York Times and another from Encyclopedia Britannica. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI | Gene Marks
events.summary: Big business has shown small firms what to do – and what not to do – with AI Small business owners have watched large companies fumble – and sometimes succeed – with AI, and then use what works O ne thing I’ve learned about corporate America is that what it succeeds at ultimately trickles down to benefit small businesses. Bleeding-edge technologies such as the internet, mobile transactions and the cloud were first perfected by large organizations – government and corporations – and now they’re available to the masses at a much lower cost and with better reliability. The good news is that it’s also the same for what they fail at. This is the lesson so far with artificial intelligence. Thanks to the billions invested – and in many cases squandered – by big brands, SMBs (small and mid-sized businesses) have learned what works, what doesn’t, where to spend and where to abstain. Small businesses should be grateful. We’re getting the answers without paying for all the mistakes. What works: AI for software development, customer service, security and voice. Big technology companies are already using AI to write, review and test code, allowing smaller development teams to accomplish more. Other firms have leaned in to AI to help with a variety of customer service processes with some success. IT departments are relying heavily on AI-enabled security platforms to detect and remedy unusual behavior, phishing attacks, and other vulnerabilities. Big brands are rolling out more AI-powered voice systems that answer incoming calls and perform rudimentary actions. Small businesses are watching. And now doing. A countless number of the developers laid off by big tech are using AI tools to replicate themselves and provide services for smaller companies on a larger scale, and we’re hiring them. Big companies have also begun to discover the astronomical computing costs that can result when employees and AI agents consume enormous numbers of tokens. Oh yes, we’ve seen that too. Small businesses like mine have watched large companies throw away billons on large-scale projects with little to show for it. We can’t afford to do the same. But we’re not scared away. Instead, we’re picking low-hanging fruit. Big companies have taught smaller businesses how not to advertise their AI investments. For months, on earnings calls and investor meetings, big company CEOs have gushed over the cost savings and headcount reductions they expect to realize with AI, and this resulted mostly in a backlash from their employees and the general public. SMBs – short of talent and long on needs – have watched and learned to do the opposite, using AI to increase productivity without lowering payroll. As a result, we have become more appealing to workers who are disgusted by the absence of loyalty and terrified over the lack of job protection at their corporate employers. We have watched corporations implement mass layoffs while using AI as their cover for their mismanagement and over-hiring, only to hire those same employees back. AI is an easy scapegoat. At my company, we’re using AI to increase productivity, not to announce payroll reductions. Thanks to larger corporations, which have struggled with the reliability and accuracy of agentic AI, SMBs have learned not to trust those agents that are supposed to be doing everything for them … yet. We’re not replacing our accounting, marketing and customer service departments anytime soon. However, we’re using AI more to help analyze our businesses, make recommendations and suggest strategies. We’ll let the big companies beta-test all those agents. We’re patient. And we don’t trust anyone, particularly bots. Most important, big corporations have taught small business owners like me to trust our guts and have faith in our common sense. All of the predictions made since ChatGPT was first introduced – mass layoffs, universal income, AGI, robots doing laundry, new worlds in the metaverse, self-driving cars – haven’t happened yet. Even OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, recently admitted that their timelines for AI adoption were “too ambitious”. He’s right. Of course there will be many changes to the way we do business in the future thanks to the progress of artificial intelligence. I’m sure there will be all sorts of tools to increase our productivity and profitability. But you know what? I’ll let the big corporations figure all that out on their dime.

events.title: I moved back into my childhood home in my 30s. I never planned to stay long, but now I'm finding it hard to leave.
events.summary: Moving back into my childhood home to live with my parents in my 30s isn't the setback I thought it would be. Meredith Schneider Four years ago, my cat and I moved into my childhood home with my parents out of necessity. It's been nice to save money and bond more with my family during this stage of life. This arrangement lasted longer than expected, and moving out feels like it's going to be tough. The day after Thanksgiving, I learned I'd have to move out of my beloved century-old, two-bedroom apartment in Kansas City. My building had been taken over by a management company in another state. Unfortunately, this wasn't the beginning of a Hallmark movie in which the protagonist unites with her neighbors to successfully push back against a corporate takeover (all while finding love along the way). Instead, I found myself panicking about my next move while grieving the comfortable life I'd been so proud to have built over the seven years I'd rented that space. A few weeks later, my parents suggested that my cat and I move back into my childhood home in the suburbs nearby. As much as living with mom and dad in my 30s felt like it could be embarrassing or a huge step back, it felt like the best choice. So, I did. I planned to stay for just a few months, but it's now been four years — and leaving feels more difficult than I ever anticipated. Financially, this setup has been a blessing Living with my parents has been going pretty well. Meredith Schneider My parents live in a home that they have been paying a mortgage on for nearly 30 years. It's much cheaper than anything on the rental market, and my financial contributions aren't even close to what I'd be paying if I lived elsewhere. It's also been freeing not to chase roommates down for their share of the rent. I've cut back on my expenses even more by no longer paying for WiFi or electric bills, and doing laundry at home instead of a laundromat. My parents have always purchased enough food for a full household, even when they were empty nesters. This means food is rarely in short supply, and my grocery bill is less , too. Luckily, they also stock up on some great snacks and subscribe to a weekly May through October Community Supported Agriculture (CSA) box full of organic produce that I cannot get enough of. To further contribute to the household, I like to offer support through physical labor and chores. Personally, I love to cook, bake, and run errands for the family. I also run errands for my grandmother, who lives close by, which helps me check in with her more regularly. Our dynamic has shifted, and I'm enjoying getting to enjoy my parents in a new way I've experienced a lot of life now that I'm in my 30s, which has helped my parents trust me to be independent. Meredith Schneider Living with my parents in my 30s is very different from when I was a kid or even a teenager. I had been away for a number of years, living in other cities and on my own, and that independence has earned me more of my parents' trust. They now realize I am too old for rules — for the most part. In time, they have backed down on strict curfews and specific chore guidelines. We've also been able to have important conversations around expectations. I've made it clear that respecting this household and keeping my parents informed about my plans is still important to me, but that it might look different now that I'm older. For example, when I first moved back, my dad was constantly checking in on me. It was difficult to deal with, especially because I'm a freelance creative with a varied social life and shifting schedule. Still, I can understand a father worrying about their kid. A brief chat about my age and level of responsibility helped us find common ground and build trust around checking in as needed. Sharing a space with my parents as an adult has also helped me see them as they are now, from a perspective that is so different and less selfish than the one I had in my adolescence. I have gotten to work alongside them and admire the career people they are firsthand. I enjoy their respective skills and hobbies, and even the lively debates we stir up while watching a new TV show. I didn't plan to stay long, but now I worry about how difficult leaving will be My parents have been pretty great roommates. Meredith Schneider Moving back home wasn't such a step backward after all. I have been able to jump into the gig economy full force, contribute regularly to the household, and spend time with family. My "few months" at home with my parents has turned into four years. Although I have plenty of savings that would allow me to move out and live comfortably, I've taken my time finding a stable living situation that makes sense for me. However, leaving home and all its comforts will be a lot harder than I thought this time around. Still, no matter where I end up, I'll continue to connect with my parents , whether taking my mom to concerts or trying new burger spots with my dad. I will also still offer to pick up sticks from the river birches in their backyard that I made them promise not to get rid of. Everyone's timeline is unique and circumstances are different. I feel lucky — not embarrassed — I've got family to fall back on. And my parents will (most likely) always be my favorite roommates. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UAE and Lebanon revive joint business council as economic ties gather pace
events.summary: The UAE and Lebanon have revived a joint business council aimed at increasing trade and investment, and developing new partnerships between companies in the two countries. The Federation of UAE Chambers of Commerce and Industry signed an agreement with the Federation of the Chambers of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture in Lebanon during the UAE-Lebanon Business Forum in Beirut, it was formally announced on Sunday. Abdallah Sultan Al Owais, vice chairman of the Federation of UAE Chambers and chairman of the Sharjah Chamber of Commerce and Industry, signed the agreement with Mohamed Choucair, chairman of the Lebanese federation. The joint UAE-Lebanon Business Council will provide a platform for exchanging market intelligence and expertise, promoting trade and investment opportunities, and developing partnerships and joint ventures. The forum, which ended on Thursday, also resulted in four agreements covering several economic areas. Discussions focused on easing market entry, encouraging two-way investment and identifying sectors offering opportunities for companies from both countries. Dr Thani Al Zeyoudi , Minister of Foreign Trade, who led an 80-member UAE delegation to Beirut, said discussions at the forum demonstrated “the readiness of UAE and Lebanese businesses to move from dialogue to partnership”. Business leaders told The National during the forum that they hoped to gain a “first-mover advantage” by investing in sectors of Lebanon's economy including logistics, agriculture, energy, aviation and tourism. The council is also expected to identify high-growth sectors and build a pipeline of investment projects and commercial ventures between UAE and Lebanese companies. Renewed ties The initiative revives a business mechanism dating back almost two decades. The UAE and Lebanese chambers signed an agreement in Beirut in 2008 to establish an Emirati-Lebanese Business Council. The latest move comes as the two countries rebuild economic ties after several years of strained diplomatic relations. The UAE has historically been a significant investor in Lebanon. Between 2003 and 2016, it was the largest source of Arab direct investment into the country, with investments worth $7.8 billion, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Relations deteriorated sharply in 2021, when the UAE withdrew its diplomats from Beirut alongside moves by Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. The dispute followed comments by Lebanon's then-information minister about the Saudi-led coalition's involvement in Yemen and broader Gulf concerns about the influence of Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon. A diplomatic reset followed the election of Joseph Aoun as Lebanon's President in January 2025, ending a vacuum that had lasted more than two years. The UAE reopened its embassy in Beirut later that month. The rapprochement gathered pace during Mr Aoun's visit to Abu Dhabi in May 2025, when the countries agreed to expand economic and investment co-operation, and establish a joint business council. The UAE also lifted restrictions on Emirati citizens travelling to Lebanon. Trade momentum Bilateral non-oil trade reached $4.2 billion in 2025, an annual increase of 35.6 per cent, according to Wam. The latest business forum brought together senior government officials and business leaders to identify investment opportunities and strengthen direct links between UAE and Lebanese companies. The council will focus on priority sectors and joint economic initiatives, while facilitating direct engagement between investors and entrepreneurs, with the aim of increasing bilateral trade and investment, and supporting new joint ventures.

events.title: I'm a psychologist who studies couples: The happiest couples never fight about this 1 thing (it's not sex or money)
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships I'm a psychologist who studies couples: 7 red flags of an 'extremely' unhealthy relationship Psychology and Relationships Psychologist: 5 things the happiest couples do in the evening—instead of watching TV How to Talk to People The most charismatic people use 5 simple phrases to get people to like them: Public speaking expert Psychology and Relationships The happiest couples do these 4 things early on—they've 'already built a roadmap,' says Harvard-trained psychologist Psychology and Relationships Do this to connect with people, says dating coach: You'll get a more 'positive response' When people ask me what causes the most damage in a relationship, they expect me to list out the usual suspects, like financial trouble or intimacy problems. And they're not wrong to guess that, since both money and sex come up constantly in research on conflict. But as a psychologist who's spent years studying couples, I've noticed something else: Couples who feel quietly resentful of each other are, in my experience, almost always running a mental ledger. They tally who cooked last night, who's more exhausted, who canceled plans last time, who "owes" whom. Whether they admit it or not, there's an invisible math humming beneath the surface of every other disagreement, and it wears down their relationships. The happiest couples I've seen, however, have stopped fighting about who's doing more. They're not keeping score in the first place. Psychologists have names for the two different operating systems a relationship can run on: In an exchange relationship , partners informally track what they give and what they get, and they expect things to even out fairly soon. For example: I did the school pickup Monday, so you're doing it Tuesday. In a communal relationship , partners give based on what the other person needs in the moment, without expecting a same-day return, trusting that things balance out over the life of the relationship rather than the day or week. Most relationships start out somewhere between the two types. What I've found tracks with a 13-year study of more than 7,000 couples: The ones who stay stuck running on exchange logic — rather than easing into something communal — see their satisfaction erode over time. Picture a couple after dinner. The kitchen's a mess, the dog needs walking, and one of them has an early flight tomorrow. In an exchange relationship, somebody's doing quiet math: "I cooked, so the dishes are yours. I walked the dog Monday and Tuesday, so it's your turn tonight." If the math doesn't check out, resentment starts building. Every dish becomes a data point. Every extra walk with the dog becomes evidence for a case nobody's officially building. No one declares themselves the treasurer of the relationship, but the books get kept anyway. In a communal relationship, the same scene plays out differently. Whoever has more energy left takes the dishes or the dog, not because a rotation says so, but because someone has to and someone can. Nobody's filing it away as a favor owed. The work still gets split roughly evenly over time — these aren't martyrs — but nobody's tracking it task by task. To be clear, real, chronic imbalance is its own problem. A 2023 review of more than 30 studies found that unequal invisible labor, which often falls predominantly on women, is tied to stress, lower life and relationship satisfaction, and negative career consequences. So pretending imbalance isn't happening — like when one partner is regularly absorbing all the work and smiling through it — just delays the same resentment that often festers in exchange relationships. Healthy couples absolutely still notice when things are lopsided. The difference is what they do with that information. They raise it as a pattern to fix together rather than a balance that needs to be repaid immediately or ammunition in an unrelated argument. The shift I see in couples that make this change is usually linguistic before it's behavioral: "You owe me" turns into "we're behind." "I did the drop-off again" turns into "mornings have been a lot for both of us lately." Research backs up the benefits of this approach: Couples who use more "we" language during conflict show healthier physiological and emotional responses while they're working through a conflict and afterward. Phrased this way, the issue stops being about one person's ledger and starts being about the team's workload — which, as it turns out, is a much easier problem to solve. Mark Travers , PhD, is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the lead psychologist at Awake Therapy , a telehealth company that provides online psychotherapy, counseling, and coaching. He is also the curator of the popular mental health and wellness website Therapytips.org .

events.title: America's next grocery shock is brewing
events.summary: America's grocery squeeze has thus far been most painfully felt in a few expensive categories, like beef, coffee and chocolate. Now, the forces pushing up food prices are starting to pile up: expensive grain, soaring fertilizer and fuel, plus unpredictable weather and raging wars. Why it matters: The next grocery price shock could hit much harder — and much wider. The big picture: Your grocery store is fed by a vast global supply chain, and pressures are building all along it. The Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars have driven up diesel prices , making it more expensive to operate farm equipment for harvesting and to truck food from suppliers to stores. The war in Iran has also disrupted fertilizer supply and price, as a large share of the world's fertilizer passes through the Strait of Hormuz. Corn and wheat prices are surging, this week hitting their highest level in three years. Bad weather has hit corn crop yields, and the Russia-Ukraine war has roiled wheat exports. Friction point: Wheat's a key ingredient in pantry staples and corn is a major animal feed, so as they go up, so can meat, dairy and eggs. The intrigue: Don't assume those soaring commodity prices are a bonanza for farmers, either. They're still getting squeezed by all the other crises. Even the president of the National Corn Growers Association told Axios Future of Energy author Ben Geman that he himself wouldn't be profitable this year. Add all these pressures to the list of already inflated food items: Instant coffee is up 15.8% year-over-year; tomatoes, 12.8%; beef roasts, 13.5%; apples, 11.1%. In the latest Economist/YouGov poll , about three-quarters of people said grocery prices are still rising where they live. Threat level: There's reason to believe it's only going to get worse. In a widely cited report earlier this month, J.P. Morgan analysts warned that global food inflation would hit 5% in the first half of 2027, nearly double what it was in the first half of 2026. "Price pressures are expected to extend through (the first half of 2027), as crop and price effects are still building and agricultural impacts lag the oceanic peak by 6 to 12 months," they wrote. The bottom line: These forces don't drive up your grocery budget overnight, but the compounding strain on the cost of growing, harvesting and transporting food is poised to make an already expensive grocery run even worse.

events.title: What new tariff walls in U.S.-Canada trade war mean for the economy's critical metals
events.summary: Metals and materials stocks surged early in the week on the eruption of a new trade war, with the U.S. imposing 50% tariffs on around $20 billion worth of imports from Canada, its second-biggest trading partner after Mexico, and Canada retaliating with equal trade measures. Metals like steel have had a strong year, buoyed not only by tariffs protecting domestic producers, but also AI data center construction. Still, the rally fizzled out and quick trade gains from sector plays mask a more complicated Trump trade war reality: complex supply chains where raw materials and parts cross back and forth over the border. As the U.S. and Canada stare down tens of billions of dollars in dueling tariff regimes as a result of President Trump's new trade war against the nation's second-biggest trading partner, companies, economists, and investors are back in the game of attempting to forecast the level of volatility to expect on corporate balance sheets and in stock prices. The U.S. government's 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods were met with Canada's $20 billion in retaliatory tariffs slated to go into effect on Sept. 8. They encompass more than 700 U.S. goods, meant to mirror the size of Trump's import taxes on Canadian wine, cement, hockey sticks and more. The counter-tariffs, which range from 15% to 50%, target a wide array of U.S. imports into Canada, including dairy, seafood, appliances, wood and paper products, and clothes. There were some real-time market winners as the new trade war dominated headlines last Monday. Consider the reaction in steel and materials stocks, including Nucor , Steel Dynamics , Cleveland-Cliffs and Century Aluminum , which all shot up on Monday after the U.S.-Canada trade talks broke down, and after many had fallen the week before on bets a new U.S-Canada deal would lower tariffs on steel and aluminum. The VanEck Steel ETF ( SLX ) rose 1.6% on Monday alone, while the State Street Materials Select Sector SPDR ( XLB ) hit an intraday all-time high — surpassing its previous all-time record price reached in February — as the metals stocks and other producers rallied. But the new trade war rally didn't last. XLB ended the five-day trading week in negative territory and SLX was close to flat. To be sure, these funds have already booked some hefty gains in 2026. Year-to-date, both ETFs are beating the S&P 500 , with SLX up over 28% and XLB up over 18%, according to Morningstar data as of Aug. 28. Atsi Sheth, chief credit officer at Moody's Ratings, said uncertainty is the watchword now. "Expect much more of this uncertainty for some time to come," Sheth said. Which businesses win in a trade war and which lose depends on an increasingly complex supply chain. One of the most complicated is the auto sector, where parts cross back and forth over the border multiple times in the production of a vehicle. "For the auto sector, our view is that the sector is so integrated that the tariffs just don't impact the country you are tariffing but your own country," Sheth said of the U.S.-Canada automobile manufacturing ecosystem. U.S. steel companies are more likely to benefit, she said, because the U.S. market is larger. "The auto sector, there are no winners. Steel ... U.S. has a little edge," Sheth said. "The new tariffs create a meaningful but manageable headwind," said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global investment strategist at Edward Jones, a headwind that cuts both ways, as higher steel and aluminum costs also start working through U.S. manufacturers, autos, and construction on this side of the border. Kyle Mohrbach, senior executive for North America automotive at o9 Solutions, a supply chain technology and consulting firm, said the greatest exposure sits in components and materials that are Canadian-sourced, single-sourced, hard to substitute, or required to keep an assembly line moving. In the automotive sector, that includes everything from steel, stampings, and powertrain components to braking systems, electronics and specialized subassemblies. Why short-term winners in trade wars are hard to trust Scott Beaulier, dean of the College of Business and professor of economics at the University of Wyoming, draws a distinction between stocks that benefit and businesses that benefit. "A tariff can create an immediate scarcity premium for domestic steel and aluminum producers. But the durable winners will be firms that have three things: domestic capacity they can bring online, relatively secure energy and raw-material inputs, and customers unable to easily substitute away from them," Beaulier said. That's a much smaller group than "American metals companies," he said. Aluminum is a good example, according to Beaulier. "The United States remains heavily import-dependent, and Canada has supplied an extraordinary share of U.S. primary aluminum.

events.title: ‘Without us, no wheel would turn’: the unsung heroes keeping England’s transport moving
events.summary: On shift, but out of sight – from ‘that person with the table tennis bats’ on the airport tarmac to remote signallers managing rail traffic Not many people get to park their car here – bang in the middle of Heathrow airport , on the taxiway just a stretch of grass away from where a line of passenger planes is coming in to land. It’s close enough to see the shimmering air and smoke as nose tyres hit the tarmac. “An A380 will put down as much rubber as a car’s entire tyre,” Jack Quantick-Thorne says. He knows – part of his job is to ensure the runway team scrapes it off and patches things up overnight. And it is all recycled, he adds. The airfield operations officer is not in the limelight much, but is one of a host of unsung workers keeping transport moving. And some jobs far from the public eye turn out to be not only essential, but surprisingly challenging. Jack Quantick-Thorne, airfield operations officer, Heathrow Passengers might only catch a glimpse of Quantick-Thorne from a window seat on landing, if he grabs the paddles to marshal a plane into the exact designated spot at the stand. “People just think you’re that person with the table tennis bats,” he grimaces slightly, as the Guardian requests a demonstration. “That’s like 5% of my job.” In fact, most planes are now brought to the stand via laser-guided electronic displays. But human marshalling remains a crucial backup. Brandishing the paddles, Quantick-Thorne beckons in a taxiing British Airways arrival, the pilot peering down from the cockpit and steering 50 tonnes of plane straight towards him. The nosewheel travels bang on the guideline, stopping exactly in position for the airbridge to swing in and allow passengers to disembark. Nerve-racking? “No. When you’ve got a really big plane, an A380, you need a second marshal right by the wheel to check it’s stopped in the right place,” he says. Back in the car, the job continues: “I’m patrolling, I’m looking around, scanning everything – is the refueller doing his job properly, has the aircraft got chocks under its wheels?” That includes monitoring the road system under Heathrow’s airfields, recognising every vehicle and checking any infringement: drivers here can also clock up points on their licence, if he spots them. Officers also need to look out for wildlife – particularly birds, a serious danger for jet planes (and vice versa). How does he deal with them? “ We’ve got methods of dispersal,” says the airfield operations officer. These, marvellously, turn out to be speakers on the roof of the van, which play a range of bird sounds: “If I saw a flock of starlings, if I played a starling noise, the starling would think, ‘Oh, maybe there’s a predator nearby,’ and they fly off.” And, he demonstrates, “I’ve got common gull. Black-headed gull. I’ve got a falcon”. Are there falcons? “No,” he explains patiently. “So you think about it from a bird’s point of view. If there’s a pigeon over there, best play a falcon so it will fly off.” If he now knows birds, it’s the planes that drew him here. He was previously at Nats, the air traffic control centre in Swanwick, managing the planes, but never up close. There is more to it than the paddles – but, he confesses, he takes every opportunity to use them, and records each plane that he has marshalled, including every aircraft in BA’s short-haul fleet. Being a pilot is the dream, he admits, but the prohibitive training costs – £100,000 or more – put it out of reach. For an enthusiast, he reckons the job is the next best thing. Last year he had to tow the Concorde that still stands at the edge of the airfield across for an exhibition: “It was the first time one had moved in years – incredible to see in the rear-view mirror.” Chris Thackaberry, network traffic controller, Transport for London The day starts in Victoria Station House overlooking the bus terminus, a grand old building that looks considerably less so inside, where Chris’s desk is surrounded by hundreds of cardboard diversion signs. About 500 of the capital’s 19,000 bus stops are on his patch in Westminster – home to some of Britain’s most congested streets, where dozens of bus routes cross. Roadworks are the bane of the bus and Thackaberry’s job is to keep them moving – armed with a van, pliers and zip ties. Sometimes he can plan for roadworks months ahead. But other days are less predictable, when life suddenly blocks a route: “It could be a broken-down vehicle or a burst water main, but I’ve had windows falling out of buildings, I’ve had a collapsed horse on a bridge. I had an upside down Lamborghini in Piccadilly … I don’t know if it was sticking to the 20mph limit.” His incident response van contains an orderly standing desk area and even a printer to rustle up more signs if needed, as well as spill dry sacks, ready to suck up any diesel or oil leaked over the road.

events.title: Icelanders reject reopening talks to join the EU despite Trump's Greenland threats
events.summary: Icelanders rejected reopening EU accession talks by 52.8% to 47.2%. Opponents centered their campaign on sovereignty and control of Iceland’s fisheries. The vote came amid heightened Arctic tensions and debate over Iceland’s strategic role in NATO. Icelanders voted to reject resuming talks to join the European Union , as issues such as domestic control over fishing appeared to override geopolitical security concerns. Broadcaster RUV reported that 52.8% of voters rejected the government's push to reopen EU membership negotiations, while 47.2% voted in favor. The question put to the Nordic nation of nearly 400,000 was whether Iceland should resume accession negotiations with the European Union. A majority "yes" vote would have led to a negotiated agreement being put to a second referendum for Icelanders to accept or reject. The debate has taken on deeper significance in the wake of U.S. President Donald Trump 's Arctic saber-rattling . But in the end, concern over the potential loss of control over its fishing industry and an erosion of national identity won out over how Iceland might be affected by geopolitical rivalries. "The 'No' side succeeded because it tapped into the most fundamental driver of Icelandic national identity: the demand for absolute self-governance. This is inextricably linked to control over natural resources and fisheries, which forms the very heart of the Icelandic understanding of sovereignty," said Eiríkur Bergmann, professor of politics at Iceland's Bifröst University. Fishing's share of Iceland's broader economy has declined over the decades, even as seafood remains a major export industry. Marine products and farmed fish made up nearly 47% of the country's exports in the August 2025-July 2026 period, according to Statistics Iceland. But production halved from a peak of 2.2 million tons in 1997 to 1.1 million tons in 2024, World Bank data show. Agriculture, forestry and fishing contributed 9.1% of Iceland's gross domestic product in 1995, but only 3.7% by 2025, as manufacturing and services grew in importance. The U.S. president has long advocated for control over neighboring Greenland on national security grounds. Notably, Trump appeared to repeatedly mix up Greenland and Iceland during a special address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier in the year. Iceland, a founding member of NATO, is the only ally without its own military forces. The country also sits astride the so-called GIUK Gap, a naval choke point between Greenland, Iceland and the U.K. that links the Arctic to the Atlantic Ocean. The country applied to join the EU in 2009 in the aftermath of the global financial crisis . A euroskeptic government suspended negotiations in 2013, and the accession process was formally ended in 2015. It's already deeply integrated into the European framework, partly through its membership of the European Economic Area, which gives the volcanic island access to the EU's single market without requiring full membership. It's also a member of the Schengen Area, which allows passport-free travel between it and other participating European countries. At the start of the year, Iceland's Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir said that deeper dialogue and collaboration with the EU would be a key factor in shoring up the country's interests. "It is clear that the international system we have lived in since the end of World War II is in turmoil," Gunnarsdottir said in an article for Icelandic newspaper Visir, according to a Google translation. "What is perhaps most striking about this referendum is that despite the profound geopolitical upheaval around us – including rapidly shifting security paradigms in the North Atlantic – these global realities never really filtered properly through into the public debate," Bifröst University's Bergmann said. "The 'Yes' side lost because they ran a highly technical and, frankly, passionless campaign." —CNBC's Sam Meredith contributed to this story.

events.title: Hospitality boom and $100 chicken nuggets: how the US Open became obscenely expensive
events.summary: Record crowds, premium seats and an unchecked resale market are transforming the self-styled people’s slam – and leaving ordinary fans fighting to get through the gates I t takes a truly exceptional affordability crisis to put Bill Ackman and Zohran Mamdani on the same side of the barricade. Yet this month the billionaire hedge fund manager and New York’s democratic socialist mayor found common cause over an unlikely grievance: the cost of getting into the US Open. Ackman took objection to the cost of a grounds pass listed for $363. Mamdani responded to the broader uproar by securing 1,000 tickets for New York residents at $100 apiece, prompting more than 336,000 people to apply for them. Somewhere between the two sits the uneasy economics of the modern US Open, where a $65 ticket with no guaranteed seat on any court can fetch more than five times that amount on the tournament’s resale marketplace. For generations the US Open has traded on its reputation as the people’s slam. Take the 7 train to Queens, buy a grounds pass and spend the day milling about within a few feet of the world’s best tennis players. But as the final major of the season begins in earnest on Sunday, that democratic ideal has been confronted with a basic problem: more and more of the people are being priced out. “The US Open is owned by the USTA which is a non-profit,” Ackman wrote on social media . “The idea that a day one ground pass is $363 is absurd. The USTA’s mission is to promote the sport of tennis. How is a $363 ground pass consistent with this mission?” It was a striking complaint from someone who rarely has reason to balk at the price of admission – in more ways than one – and more striking still when Mamdani weighed in days later. The two men have spent much of the past year fighting from opposite sides of New York’s affordability debate, with Ackman sparing no expense to prevent Mamdani’s election last November. Apparently all it took to set aside months of political blood sport for a temporary detente was the obscene cost of getting into the tennis. Heartbreaking , indeed. The simplest explanation for the US Open sticker shock is also the most obvious: demand has exploded. But so, too, has what the USTA is selling. Over the past decade the Open has transformed itself into something closer to a three-week New York cultural festival, a late-summer collision of sport, fashion, celebrity and conspicuous consumption. The $23 Honey Deuce is no longer merely a cocktail but a souvenir, status marker and social media prop. Celebrities fill the suites, influencers populate sponsor boxes and Arthur Ashe Stadium can feel less like the main show court than an aperitif to fashion week . The Open surpassed one million visitors for the first time in 2024 and shows little sign of slipping back below that mark. Everybody wants in because everybody else wants in. And there is little indication the Open intends to resist that momentum. Craig Tiley arrived this summer as the USTA’s new chief executive after more than two decades running Tennis Australia and the Australian Open, where he presided over that tournament’s similar evolution into a sprawling three-week sports and entertainment festival. He is already talking expansively about what the US Open could become. Asked Saturday how the tournament may continue to grow, Tiley offered a striking shorthand for his vision. “This will become the tennis Disneyland,” he said, a phrase unlikely to reassure the sport’s traditionalists. Growth, he explained, would come not necessarily from making the event longer but from creating more experiences for players, children and adults within it. Tiley described the “insatiable appetite” to come to Flushing Meadows as a “nice problem”, though he acknowledged there were limits to how far attendance itself should grow. “We’re not going to be one of those events that just want to pack the precinct for the sake of packing it,” he said. Unfortunately, for many longtime attendees, the same demand powering the Open’s expansion is also reshaping the economics of getting inside. As countless World Cup tourists came to discover the expensive way, New York law allows tickets to be resold for whatever someone is willing to pay, and Ticketmaster, the Open’s official ticketing partner, operates both sides of the transaction: selling the original ticket and hosting the marketplace where it can be resold. The USTA benefits from both. It acknowledges receiving a portion of Ticketmaster’s fees when a verified resale ticket changes hands, meaning the same ticket can generate revenue for the organization more than once. The USTA says its share comes from fees rather than the resale price itself, but declined to answer questions from the Guardian about what percentage it receives or how much the arrangement generates annually. The USTA argues that shutting down Ticketmaster resale would simply push buyers toward less secure third-party platforms.

events.title: The 'choose your own adventure' earnings: Why retailers are handling tariff refunds so differently
events.summary: Retailers have diverged on how they've reported tariff refunds in their earnings this quarter after applying for repayments earlier this year when President Donald Trump's duties were struck down. While some companies explicitly said they used the extra cash to lower prices for consumers, other companies said they deployed it to boost their margins. That divergence may be due to retailers taking different paths to appealing to their core consumer or investors. Tariff refunds have muddied retailers' earnings reports in recent weeks as Wall Street struggles to parse through the confusion. Most major retailers applied for refunds after the Supreme Court ruled in February that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize President Donald Trump to impose the tariffs. That money began flowing in during the second quarter, as retailers saw major boosts to their profits. For the most part, those returns have helped companies offset cost inflation and prop up margins, especially as they face cost pressures like the rising price of fuel. But the way those retailers have reported those refunds and incorporated them into their earnings has differed greatly, leading to confusion about how to read the strength of their results and their future outlooks. "These trails aren't always clean in terms of finding the right way to apply, in a fair sense, the rebate to prices," Bryan Eshelman, a managing director in the retail practice at consulting firm AlixPartners, told CNBC. Eshelman said there are two factors at play with how retailers handled the refunds. Determining where the extra money goes depends largely on the retailer's price position in the market, where more value-driven companies are likely to apply funds to keep prices lower and "proclaim that to the marketplace," he said. The tariff refund situation has been further complicated for companies depending on whether they are the importer of record for the products, which determines who gets the refunds, Eshelman said. Much of what's sold in stores isn't necessarily imported by the retailer, or U.S. manufacturers may be the ones receiving rebates for raw materials. "There's also just the reality of record-keeping internal to retailers and whether or not they easily have a way to attribute the rebate directly back to a product that was already sold," he said. "It's not a simple task." Some retailers chose to explicitly say they were dedicating their extra cash to lowering prices on products for consumers. Home Depot saw its gross margin increase 0.3% in its fiscal second quarter compared with the prior year, driven by its tariff refund. The company said it received $730 million in tariff refunds during the period, using roughly $685 million of that money to reduce the cost of goods sold. Chief Financial Officer Richard McPhail said on a call with analysts that those funds represent "the vast majority" of what the company was expecting to receive. Walmart took a similar route. CFO John David Rainey told CNBC last week that the company was eligible to receive roughly $2.9 billion in tariff refunds and has yet to get back just under $100 million of that total. Its gross profit for Walmart U.S. grew 1.6% from the boost. He told CNBC that the company plans to use those funds to lower prices for consumers, and shoppers and investors will see the impact during its current fiscal third quarter. TJX Cos. also said it used its $331 million in tariff refunds to benefit its second-quarter cost of sales. Eshelman said low-price operators likely have a "strategic reason" to apply refunds to prices, though enticing consumers with value has become harder in an increasingly crowded retail space. "At the end of the day, a product is worth what somebody's willing to pay for it, and there is a lot of choice in this marketplace," Eshelman said. Lowe's , on the other hand, said its tariff refund gave it an 11-cent boost to its earnings per share for the second quarter. CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC the company received roughly $80 million in repayments and did not plan to use tariff dollars to lower prices, unlike some of its competitors. "We feel strongly that we want to deliver strong profitability for our shareholders and make sure that we don't follow any aggressive pricing action," he said. Ellison added on a call with analysts that the company took "the right planned steps to drive profitability" with its windfall. Target also did not explicitly say whether the company was using its tariff refunds to cut prices, though the company said it lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in the second quarter. Still, the retailer said tariff refunds gave it a $752 million boost to net earnings, or $1.65 per share, and a $994 million pretax benefit to its second-quarter gross margin and operating income.

events.title: My grandkids fight bedtime with their parents. They fall asleep in minutes for me, and I try not to be smug about it.
events.summary: The author has a knack for getting her grandbabies to fall asleep. Courtesy of the author My adult kids often ask me to take over when their children won't sleep. I follow the parents' routines while staying calm and adjusting to each child's needs. Sometimes I walk out of the bedroom with a sleeping grandchild just minutes later. I must have inherited my mother's magic touch for putting kids to sleep. It drives my kids crazy. While I was visiting my son and daughter-in-law recently, she confided that bedtime had become a nightmare . I offered to give her a break by putting my grandson to bed. I was prepared for a struggle since we were at their house, and he knew his mom was in the next room. We took him to his room after his bath to put on his PJs and sleep sack . It was already darkened and droning with white noise. After she left the room, I gave him a hug and kiss while softly telling him I loved him and that it was now time for dodo. I put him down, and that was that. He squirmed a bit, but I rubbed his back for a couple of minutes until he settled down. Then I sat on the bed opposite his crib and read on my phone until he fell asleep. No hassle, no crying, no standing up. This is not the first occurrence. Frequently, my exasperated kids have relinquished naptime to me when visiting. It is understood by everyone that Grand-maman will put the children to sleep . I try not to react smugly to their parents' astonishment as I walk out of the sleeping child's room five minutes later. Calm is contagious Rocking a baby to sleep remains one of my favorite and calming things in the world. As a young mother, I would especially look forward to those breaks, justifying my taking all the time I needed to put my child to sleep and glean some much-needed serenity myself. For babies, my strategies consist of following their parents' lead. I stay on top of their current routine and stick to their order of things. Bathtime, quiet time, dark rooms , a pacifier, a bottle, a soft blanket, or a special plushie are no-brainers. After running through their usual preliminaries, I sit in the bedroom rocking chair, holding them just firmly enough to help them settle without restricting movement so much that it provokes a struggle. I create sensory rhythmic patterns with my breathing, humming, patting, or rubbing circles on their back. Usually, that works. If not, small adjustments like standing and swaying, or switching from rubbing to patting and vice versa, are often enough. Once I have found a successful method for one child, I stick to it the next time. I am gentle but firm and use all of my tricks If they do start to fuss, it is important not to let it escalate to the point of prolonging the process. Sometimes, taking a break and trying again is necessary. I ask myself: Is he overtired? Not tired enough? When was his last sleep and for how long? Is he feeling well? Has there been an abnormal disruption that threw him off his routine? I let those answers guide my next steps. If the child is upset or unwell, I take him to another room to help him reset, dimming the lights and turning off anything noisy. For older kids, negotiation is often necessary. I remind them why quiet time is important: we have more fun later when we're not grumpy. I offer to read a story or play a children's meditation or story from my phone. I lay beside them in a darkish, quiet room and intentionally take loud, deep rhythmic breaths to encourage them to mimic me. The younger ones usually fall asleep, but the older ones who have outgrown naps at least rest, which is always helpful. Different strokes for different little folks It is important to remember that each child is different. Some like to be rocked, some like to be laid down with a back rub, and others like to stand and sway. I adapt to whatever works for them and stick to it. Consistency is key. I usually wait until they are calmed down, then ease them into bedtime with whatever feels familiar and comforting. Sometimes that’s rocking and humming; sometimes it’s just staying close and reassuring them until they settle. If they resist, I keep it gentle and remind him that it’s bedtime and that Grandma loves them. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Saudi firms pull IPO plans
events.summary: The Scoop Three Saudi companies have scrapped plans for initial public offerings that were scheduled over the next month because of expectations of weak investor demand as the Iran war weighs on sentiment, according to people familiar with the matter. The decision suggests the companies believe that foreign investors remain wary of putting new money into the kingdom’s stock exchange, and will likely put off other firms planning IPOs in the short term. That will be a blow to the owners of companies that were considering going public, including Public Investment Fund. The three companies — bottled drinks company Berain Water, lubricants and automobile servicing business Petrolube, and Facilities Management Company — have made the decision in recent days in coordination with the Capital Market Authority (CMA), the regulator, the people said. The CMA is also keen to make sure the first IPOs under new chairman, Mazen Al Sudairi, are a success, according to one of the people. Berain and Petrolube declined to comment; CMA and Facilities Management didn’t respond to requests for comment. Know More Earlier this year construction company Mutlaq Al Ghowairi pulled a share sale because of weak investor demand. The deal, which would have valued the company at $799 million, was the first significant IPO to test investor appetite in Saudi since the onset of the Iran war in February. PIF had been considering a fresh wave of stock offerings in companies it controls this year and next, pinning its hopes on a stock market revival as a way to raise cash to fund new investments. Under the CMA’s rules, firms are given a six month window to complete a share sale after receiving approval from the regulator. If they don’t complete an offering within that timeframe they have to restart the process. The three firms that just put their IPO plans on hold have until the end of September to either complete an offering or reapply to the regulator for listing approval. The companies are expected to reapply for IPO approval when market conditions improve, the people familiar with the matter said. Gulf markets have been volatile since the Iran conflict began, with the Saudi bourse recovering initial losses to be up almost 7% since the start of the year. The bourse declined more than 12% last year. The Dubai Financial Market is down nearly 3% over the same period, and the main Abu Dhabi index is up by 0.4%. Notable Saudi Arabia’s stock market regulator is investigating the poor performance of recent IPOs, including looking into the advice given by investment banks as it tries to kickstart new listings, Semafor reported .

events.title: Russia is slowly grinding through the Donbas as Ukraine braces for a brutal fight over its last strongholds
events.summary: A Ukrainian soldier looks out of a window of an apartment destroyed by shelling in the direction of Kostiantynivka. Alex Nikitenko/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Russia is advancing slowly through the Donbas as Ukraine prepares to defend its last major strongholds. Ukrainian commanders say the fight for Kramatorsk and Sloviansk could become brutal battles of attrition. Analysts warn the outcome may hinge on Ukraine's ability to keep troops supplied under relentless drone and air attacks. There is a moment before the camera begins rolling when the young Ukrainian commander says, "History is repeating itself for us in the Donbas. Unfortunately." Then he falls silent. A few minutes later, the man, known by the call sign "Fleshka," takes a seat on a weight bench in the garden of a house in an eastern Ukrainian village, just a 30-minute drive from the nearest Russian troops. Every morning, he benches 80 kilograms here before returning to the screens where he coordinates the destruction of Russian assault units through the live feeds from his drone operators. "I hope it will be a long fight. This is our land, and we will fight for every meter of it," Fleshka says once the camera is rolling. A few meters away stands his comrade "Sascha," another unit commander with the 33rd Brigade. "It's going to be a brutal meat grinder," he predicts, describing a bloody war of attrition. "But I'm glad to be part of it." Fleshka, 24, and Sascha, 26, belong to a new generation of young Ukrainian commanders helping lead the defense of the last Ukrainian-held bastions in the Donbas. Both have spent years fighting on the front lines. They were involved in the drawn-out Battle of Bakhmut in 2023 and later took part in Ukraine's offensive in Russia's Kursk region at the end of 2024. Today, each man is responsible for more than 80 soldiers serving in a combined drone-and-infantry unit. "Fleshka," a young Ukrainian commander, speaking with WELT in eastern Ukraine. Lysenko/WELT The Donbas is comprised of the Luhansk and Donetsk regions. Russia has captured almost all of Luhansk, while Ukraine controls just under one-fifth of the Donetsk region, an area of roughly 5,000 square kilometers, about five times the size of Berlin. The question is increasingly not whether Putin's army will seize the remaining Ukrainian-held territory in Donbas, but when. According to information obtained by WELT from conversations with representatives of a leading European intelligence service, Russian forces could reach the outskirts of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by early 2027. The two cities form the center of the last major Ukrainian defensive belt in the Donbas. Intelligence officials predict that Russian troops could complete the conquest of most of the region by next year. The human cost of that campaign, however, would likely be staggering. Hundreds of thousands more Russian soldiers could be killed or seriously wounded in the process. Since the start of the war in 2022, Russia's military has suffered around 1.4 million casualties, according to estimates by analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, including up to 450,000 dead and nearly one million wounded. Military analyst Franz-Stefan Gady, author of Attack: When War Comes to Us , offers a somewhat more optimistic assessment for Ukraine. Russia's advance , he argues, is progressing at its slowest pace since winter. "At the current rate, Donetsk region would not be fully captured until the early 2030s," he says. Ukrainian service members in the heavily contested city of Pokrovsk, an area of intense fighting in Donetsk. Alex Nikitenko/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images A slowdown, however, should not be mistaken for a stabilization of the front lines. In some sectors, Kyiv's military position is deteriorating. Russia enjoys local superiority in first-person-view drones on certain stretches of the front, in some cases by a ratio of 10 to one. Meanwhile, 3,000-kilogram guided glide bombs continue to inflict heavy losses on Ukrainian forces in front-line areas. Gady believes it's possible that Russian troops could reach Kramatorsk and Sloviansk as early as spring or summer 2027, but only under one condition. "Russia needs mobilization if it wants to sustain or increase the current pace," he says. "Moscow is unlikely to do this before the elections, and if it does, Ukraine has no equivalent response available." According to Gady, Russia's General Staff estimates that newly mobilized troops need around four months before they can have a meaningful impact at the front. A mobilization this autumn could therefore begin to shape events during the first half of 2027. Col. Markus Reisner of the Austrian Armed Forces says Russia's summer offensive has so far fallen well short of Kremlin expectations. Nevertheless, Putin's troops continue to advance "slowly but steadily". The decisive factor in the battle for the Donbas, he argues, will be Ukrainian logistics. "The single most important capability influencing the fight for the Ukrainian defensive belt around Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is the ability to supply the defenders in those cities. If Russian forces succeed in disrupting those supply routes, Ukrainian defenders will be able to hold out only for a limited period." A Ukrainian service member in Druzhkivka, one of the three cities making up the fortress belt in Donetsk. Pierre Crom/Getty Images Already, much of the resupply effort relies on heavy multicopter drones and uncrewed ground vehicles . Russian forces are systematically targeting these systems while simultaneously attempting to prevent the reinforcement and rotation of Ukrainian troops. Reisner's warning is stark: "If the Ukrainians fail to break this vicious cycle, the defensive belt will fall." Ukrainian brigade commanders also acknowledge that Russia ultimately possesses the resources required to conquer the Donbas. "Of course, Russia has the potential," Vadym Krykun, commander of the Lubart Brigade, told WELT earlier this year. "It remains the second-largest army in the world. The question is how far Russia is willing to go, how much further it is prepared to mobilize its economy and its population." Krykun has been fighting in Donbas for more than a decade. Russian troops first entered the region in 2014, and fighting has continued ever since. As recently as last year, there were hopes that a settlement over eastern Ukraine might pave the way for a ceasefire or even peace. At the end of 2025, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed withdrawing Ukrainian troops from parts of the Donbas as part of a peace initiative, on the condition that Russia also withdraw and that the area be converted into an internationally monitored demilitarized zone, or "free economic zone." The Kremlin rejected the proposal, which was also supported by the United States. events.title: I knew my job wasn't the right fit for me. It still took me a year to quit.
events.summary: The author knew she needed to quit her job, and her husband was supportive. Courtesy of Kate Oczypok My people-pleasing tendencies kept me in a job that wasn't the right fit for too long. I prefer more structure and feedback than I was getting, and needed a change. After quitting, family and friends have said I seem lighter and happier. As the oldest of five children, I've always seen things through. I've been the responsible one, the one who gets it done, and, most importantly, a self-imposed people-pleaser . These are just a few of the reasons it was so hard to quit a job that I devoted a decade to. As a freelance writer , it's sometimes hard to find work, let alone steady work. I knew I could count on this position, but I also knew my mental health was being affected by it. There was less structure than what I preferred, and it just wasn't a good fit for me or the way I prefer to work, which includes plenty of routine, organization, and feedback. It took me some time to come to a decision I stuck it out for a while, constantly weighing whether to quit or stay. Staying meant a consistent income, continuing to contribute to my household, and having financial security (or as much as freelancing can give!). Quitting meant no financial security , and given my people-pleasing nature, I was terrified of leaving my other coworkers. I was even more scared of what future employers would think about my decision. To quit or not to quit was a question I pondered for over a year. Since I was so indecisive and constantly worried about this choice, I knew my mental health was suffering. I was worried all the time, I had insomnia, gastrointestinal issues, and my often anxiety-induced epilepsy had reared its ugly head. Finally, my husband and I talked, and he mentioned how he had been observing how upset I was. Earlier in the year, we had decided I'd stick it out until I found other work with similar pay. I had yet to find that other work, though, which made my decision even more nerve-racking. During our conversation, my husband talked about how he would support me if I quit , and we'd figure things out as we always did. He just wanted to see me happy and less stressed. That was very reassuring, but my perfectionism continued to rear its ugly head. My husband said he'd supported my decision, and a therapy session solidified it During a late May therapy session, I was discussing this yet-to-be-determined decision. My therapist saw how exasperated I was and simply and bluntly asked: "What is keeping you there?" She also reminded me that people leave jobs all the time for many reasons, and there was no reason to worry. It was a total lightbulb moment. I decided then and there that I was going to quit. The very next week, I left the organization. It was a scary, yet oddly refreshing feeling. I felt free and excited for the next chapter. A tradition my husband has kept up for years is handwritten letters to me on my birthday and our anniversary. A lot of my July birthday letter talked about how he knew my decision wasn't easy, but he was proud that I did it. He said quitting was a brave thing to do, and he loved me even more for doing it. After quitting, I've been happier and have had opportunities come my way Since I left the organization, I have had so many opportunities come my way. Naturally, most of my worries have dissipated, even though there is still some financial uncertainty as I finish out the year. Family and friends have said I sound lighter and happier. I've been writing regularly for a few publications, and now I have more time to pitch publications and search for jobs. My decision was the best idea for me, as it helped with my mental health and made me more inspired and excited for what's to come than ever before. It also reiterated how my husband and I are a team, and sometimes when one of us is down, the other steps up, and vice versa. All in all, the phrase "you got this" was something I repeated multiple times throughout this process. Now, I'm looking forward to whatever comes next. Read the original article on Business Insider
