events.title: I bought a fixer-upper for $347,000 and turned it into two Airbnbs. It went so well I turned the garage into two more.
events.summary: Vanessa Banh turned a garage on her property into two Airbnb units. Courtesy of Vanessa Banh Vanessa Banh bought her first home but never planned on living in it. Bahn turned the four-bedroom home into two Airbnb properties, then turned the garage into two more. She said she'd rather make extra money than live in one of the units. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Vanessa Banh , 28, a former accountant turned entrepreneur who bought a four-bedroom house with a garage in Modesto, California, and turned it into four separate Airbnb properties. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I feel like my generation is half and half on whether they want to own a home . Personally, I think it's really expensive now compared to our parents' generation . The cost of living and our wages compared to the cost of housing is just outrageous. For me, I was always looking for different ways to get more money. I listened to a lot of real estate people and gurus, and thought owning a house was the way to go to build assets and real wealth long-term. So why not start now if I can? I bought a house for $347,000 in 2022 as a fixer-upper and took my time. It was actually a cash or hard-money loan-only sale. I had a friend who's a hard money lender, and he looked at the property, and he was like, "I can lend this for you." So we purchased it through him through hard money. Then we were able to refinance it back out to a conventional loan within a month because it wasn't bad; it was just really old and needed some updating. I knew later on I was going to turn it into a rental. A side-by-side image of the garage before and after renovation. Courtesy of Vanessa Banh If you want to buy a house through the conventional route, you have to live in it for at least a year before you turn it into a rental. The renovations took a year and a half, so that met the criteria already. We closed in May 2022, but we didn't really start working on the renovations until August. My dad and I handled the renovations, took our time, and finished in July 2023. I was just thinking about a long-term rental, but during the renovation process, my dad had different subcontractors walk through and give us some ideas. I was also listening to a lot of podcasts — "Biggerpockets" and all that stuff — so I was like, "This could be an Airbnb." Maybe six or eight months into the process, I thought, "Let's try to Airbnb this thing and see how it goes." My first two Airbnbs were successes, so I turned my garage into two more Renovations cost about $60,000. We had to replace the roof and add a whole new AC, so those were the biggest costs. Everything else was just standard flooring, a new bathroom, new tile, and all that stuff. When we were renovating the house, one of the subcontractors who my dad had brought up to help with one part of the rental said, "In this section of the house, you could literally make this its own little unit right here." The layout was really perfect for it because there's already a door there, so all we had to do was just add a little stove and a little sink, and add a double lock on the door so it functioned as a separate unit. So now there are two units in the house. One of the units was rented out mostly for traveling professionals, which I didn't anticipate. Traveling nurses would come and stay for three months at a time — there was basically no vacancy. I didn't realize there was something called mid-term rentals . So I was like, "Wow, this is actually quite amazing." I averaged about $3,500 to $4,500 in revenue. Cash flow was about $1,000 to $1,500 because my mortgage was about $2,000 and utilities and all that stuff was about $500. The garage mid-renovation. Courtesy of Vanessa Banh. I had a garage on the property that was just collecting dust. When I bought this house, I was already imagining how we could turn that garage into an ADU . But it was more like, "How do I get enough money to build this out?" I feel like the little unit in the back was working really well for me, and it seemed like there was a lot of demand for traveling nurses and traveling professionals. My one-bedroom, one-bathroom unit was already going for $1,800, so I thought, if I can squeeze in two studios in the garage, I can get almost more than $1,800 times two. It took me a few years of stacking cash. After the renovation for the first two units was done, I started learning how to wholesale and flip homes . I was learning and actively doing that, and then I got enough cash to finally be able to start the next renovation process. Once my plans were all done and final, I got three bids from contractors and started the renovation in November 2025. I always hoped that I would finish the garage conversion by the end of 2026. We finished in January 2026 — my contractor moved really fast. The contractor's bid was about $100,000. After it was completely done, I paid another $8,500 because of miscellaneous costs, the city fees, and the architect's design. The construction debt will be paid off in a few years, but it felt like the right move I finished construction for the garage units in January, then I finished furnishing everything and getting it all ready for Airbnb by late February. In March, I started getting my first bookings. For the first few months, I had a new-listing discount because if you have no reviews on Airbnb, it's harder for guests to book it. So to make it a little more competitive, I had a lower rate. I was bringing in about $1,600 to $1,800 per unit for the first few months. But essentially, right now I'm getting about $2,000 each for the units, so I doubled the revenue I could make. Of course, it also cost almost double for the construction because of the permits — I had to pay for two permits and all that because it's two ADUs . I'm kind of paying myself off right now. I think it's going to take about two years to just pay that whole debt off, and then after that, it'll be fully cash-flowed. The interior of one of the garage Airbnbs. Courtesy of Vanessa Banh. I view real estate as a way to get ahead. I can absolutely live in one of my units, but if I can make money off of it — another $2,000 a month — I would rather do that right now. That's where my head's at right now. I was like, "How do I optimize the current home that I have to make me more money?" Because I don't have a W-2, what can I do to help myself get into a better financial position? I knew the first step was to own a home. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: My sister and I were laid off around the same time. We started a small business together to survive unemployment.
events.summary: The author and her sister run a small business, selling vintage items. Courtesy of Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein My sister and I were both laid off from our jobs around the same time as our parents died. We decided to start a small business, selling vintage items, which is something our mom taught us. The small business is helping us through unemployment and face the grief. When I walk into a suburban mid-century house with my sister, we're on the hunt for treasures that will make our customers happy — but we also like to marvel at the elaborate wallpaper in the bathroom. We have time now to sift through the junk drawers and basement bookshelves. Within the last few years, we both were laid off from our jobs as writers and editors. While we continue to fling our résumés into the ring, we keep ourselves busy at estate sales and thrift stores. We come from a family of thrifters and estate-sale lovers; our mother was an avid collector with an eye for beautiful and valuable antiques. She taught her three daughters how to find treasures in the junk —what to look for, how to bargain, and which cleaning potions worked best to restore items to their former glory. I've always enjoyed the thrill of the hunt, but I never imagined turning our shared love for vintage into a small business . My sister and I were laid off I sensed a wave of layoffs coming in digital media before it happened. A strange mix of optimism and despair coursed through me as I tried to regroup. I quickly landed a new job, only to be let go from that role a year later. Meanwhile, my younger sister had lost her job as part of mass layoffs at a major corporation. We were both reeling while grieving the loss of our mother and now also caring for our elderly father in our childhood home. With the looming threat of AI , the job market looked bleak. Layoffs disrupt and disorient. It's hard to know how to spend your time when there's suddenly so much of it. It's easy to sink into the couch and think your new job is just remembering to shower and watching every episode of " Love Island ." Facing job loss — and the grief of losing both of our parents within six years — my younger sister and I first reviewed our mom's epic collection for items we could sell. We also started hitting estate sales, thrift shops, antique malls, and garage sales more frequently. Starting a business together was the answer As we gathered more goods, I decided to make it official and established Travel Far Now Vintage, an Etsy shop , in 2023. I handle most aspects of the business — packing, shipping, and accounting — and I rely on the keen curatorial eye of my younger sister, who can walk into any estate sale or thrift shop and score the most unusual vintage items hidden in the heaps. Together, we found unexpected joy during some of the most challenging years of our lives. The sisters are always on the hunt for vintage items. Courtesy of Amanda Leigh Lichtenstein There's no shortage of tasks to fill the time — from sourcing to cleaning, listing to packing, shipping to accounting, posting, and connecting with new clients — the business keeps us energized against the lethargy of layoffs. Consistency is key. While we continue to search for meaningful full-time roles , running a vintage business keeps us alert, active, and curious about the objects we collect within an ever-changing marketplace. Luckily, no two days are alike. There's always someone looking for that exact vintage object that connects them with the past. The business has also helped us heal Running a vintage business is the ultimate crash course in grief, with lessons on letting go at every turn. There's an alchemy to this work. By giving abandoned objects a second chance at life, I've developed a deeper appreciation for the fleeting nature of time. I've come to think of myself as a "memory merchant," dealing in nostalgia through vintage objects and the stories they tell about our lives. When a client reaches out to me about an analog Sunbeam timer for sale, it's not just about the timer, but about connecting with a core memory in their childhood kitchen. Hearing these stories helps me connect with my own memories and make peace with the past. Our vintage shop is an ode to our mother — the ultimate thrifter and sifter — who taught us the ropes. When we're out shopping, we always hear our mom's voice in the aisles. "Do you know what this is?" she asks with a twinkle in her eye. "Yes, Mom, we know," we answer, and continue scanning the shelves for more unique treasures. Operating this small vintage business with my sister has strengthened our bond as we remember our mom together. The search alone is therapeutic, but it's also immensely healing to know we can breathe new life into old things. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Inside Meta’s push to put robots to work in data centers
events.summary: Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers , according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars . Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment. In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.” Read full article Comments

events.title: I spoke to 6 people who bounced back from a career break. These 3 lessons stuck with me.
events.summary: Natasya Pawanteh pivoted careers after caring for her parents. Joshua Paul for BI Business Insider's reporter Charissa Cheong spent hours interview people who took career breaks. She turned the interviews into her series My Big Break, which explores how the people bounced back. She learned a lot from the interviewees, including how sacrifice can be character-building. Over the past four months, I've spent hours interviewing people who were brave enough to take a career break. I wanted to know if and how they overcame the many obstacles career returners face when trying to crack the job market. It all built up to the series My Big Break , which told a diverse range of stories, from stepping away to care for a child with autism, caring for parents until their final breaths, and moving to another country with family and leaving a job behind. As someone who isn't planning a career break any time soon, one thing I didn't expect was to learn so much from the people who shared their stories with me. Although their journeys weren't always smooth, I took comfort in seeing how they adapted, found ways to move forward in their careers, and learned lessons that shaped their character. Here are three lessons I learned. 1. Your network can help your career comeback In my fantasy career break, I'd be offline and unplugged as much as possible. But the more interviews I did, the more I noticed how big a difference staying in touch with one's network can make in a comeback. Nicki Schroeder took a career break to care for her daughter. Hanna-Katrina Jedrosz for BI When Nicki Schroeder, a UK-based media lawyer, tried to re-enter her industry after 10 years, her contacts helped her get back up to speed, meaning she was prepared for her successful job interview . The same contacts then equipped her with a list of key precedents decided while she was out of the workforce. Talking to Schroeder made me reflect on how significant help from people you know and trust can be, especially when you feel a bit rusty after taking time off. In the case of Ramya Ramesh, a semiconductor professional who worried she'd never get another job after a six-year career break, her former colleagues encouraged her to apply for an opportunity in her old department. Meanwhile, Adam Stewart, an ex-Googler who took an eight-month break, said that he turned to former colleagues for advice about his next steps, while also making new connections. Ramya Ramesh took advantage of her previous employer's returner program. Brian W. Fraser for BI 2. A career break is an opportunity to open yourself up to new things Not all of the people I spoke to returned to their original industry. Mounika Chinnam and Natasya Pawanteh both felt reentering their industries would be challenging after long absences. The tech industry had transformed significantly during Chinnam's seven-year break, so she was open to non-technical jobs. Becoming an intern for a digital marketing company at 31 with colleagues who were younger than her felt a little strange, but it enabled her to land a full-time role in a new industry. Natasya Pawanteh changes careers. Joshua Paul for BI Pawanteh thought it would be an uphill battle getting anyone in geology to give her a chance after a seven-year break. She tried volunteering, leading to her transition into nonprofit work. Seeing how happy Pawanteh and Chinnam seemed in their new industries, which they may not have landed in had they not taken a career break, made me consider the value of trying new things and keeping an open mind. I felt similarly inspired when I met Glenn Stephenson, who took a break from his "safe" career at PwC to experiment with his own business. I like to think of myself as open to new things, but seeing someone take such a big leap made me question how far I'd go to explore an idea or passion. 3. Sacrifice can be character-building I'm still at a relatively early stage in my career, and my friends and I often discuss whether we'd want to pause work when we have kids. I've never been sure how to answer, partly because my parents worked while I was growing up. Meeting people like Schroeder and Pawanteh, who stepped back to become carers , gave me an insight into the costs and sacrifices that come with pausing a fruitful career to invest in someone else. Hearing about the energy and effort they expended, I felt challenged by how, as good as having a fulfilling job is, our collective focus on climbing corporate ladders, getting promoted, and garnering likes on LinkedIn can make us quite self-centered. It's something Pawanteh captured well when she talked about why she decided not to return to her geology career. To quote from her as-told-to essay: "I'd loved geology since I was 16, but I realized I had a selfish outlook on life, all about me, me, me. Caring for my parents made me realize what it's like to be present for another human being." Her story in particular made me hope that, if there came a time when a loved one needed me, I'd have the love and selflessness required to put my career aside for them. As Pawanteh said of her parents in her as-told-to essay: "It was a privilege to look after them until the end of their days, and I think that will be the greatest achievement of my life." You can read all the stories mentioned here in Business Insider's series, My Big Break . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘It’s therapy by stealth’: the adult fans helping Lego build its billions in sales
events.summary: A growing number of people are rediscovering their love of plastic bricks in later life and boosting the Danish company’s bottom line I n a cosy cafe in Kingston upon Thames on the outskirts of London, nine people gather in the early evening to drink and talk. To the casual observer it may look like a book club, but when the friends reach into their bags it’s not paperbacks they produce – but packs of Lego . Geoff Lay, who organised the gathering, worked in software development before recently starting Noble Brick, a Lego-focused events organisation. “I was one of those kids where you couldn’t go into my bedroom because the floor was covered in pieces,” he says. But after a break with the hobby, the 44-year-old rediscovered Lego 10 years ago – after being given a set recreating London’s Tower Bridge. He has been building ever since. The allure of a Lego set may conjure childhood fun, but a growing number of adult enthusiasts is one of the reasons behind a surge in sales which has helped increase the Danish toymaker’s revenues by 21% . Thanks to collaborations with the likes of the World Cup and Stranger Things, as well as mini figures of popular football players, more and more are finding themselves returning to the brand in later life. The Lego Group was founded in 1932 and has built a lucrative plastic empire, generating £4.8bn in revenue in the first half of 2026 alone. Since the 1990s, Lego has expanded its products to include brand tie-ins, video games, television shows and sets tailored towards adults – often costing hundreds of pounds. Lay is confident that a new demographic of older Lego enthusiasts is here to stay. He says: “The idea that Lego is for kids is banished.” His 40-year-old fiancee, Lauren Marshall, agrees: “You don’t have a typical Lego fan any more.” Marshall “didn’t have Lego as a child”, but got into the hobby as an adult after her partner’s fervour rubbed off on her. As she assembles the legs of a large Darth Vader, she says sets are “a lot like jigsaws”, and they are “completing something like a puzzle”. Someone who was raised on a less structured style of Lego play is 28-year-old Loretta Piare. “Growing up, I loved Lego. We always had huge boxes of it,” she says, as she constructs a cactus from the company’s botanical series. “We could never afford one of the fancy sets. My mum would get the big boxes of mixed colours.” She stopped playing with Lego in her teens – “I used to love building houses and making it up” – but the cost-effective and environmentally conscious option to borrow other people’s bricks at adult groups has revived her interest. “I love following instructions,” she says, “I love colourful bricks, basically. I love building things.” Tim Stone, a 35-year-old decorator, renewed his love for Lego after quitting smoking during Covid and buying himself a racing car set. While constructing a brick-based Nintendo Game Boy console, he explains how he joined the London Afol (Adult Fans of Lego) group to make new friends. “I got really bored. I had a load of buddies that would just go out drinking.” Now, Stone takes part in collaborative builds late into the night with more than 20 other Afol members. There are dozens of Lego fan groups across the UK. Jordan Wiltshire, 32, is a member of GertLUG, a “Lego user group” based in Bristol. He became conscious of the cost and began to wonder if Lego was a “sensible” purchase. When a friend bought him a Lego Star Wars Tie Fighter for Christmas when he was 26, things slotted back into place. He calls Lego his “personality”, and is a strong advocate against ageism related to the hobby. “Why can’t we play with Lego?” he asks. “Some people might say it’s for kids but there are so many of us and we all have different things we love about it.” Wiltshire, who builds his own Lego creations, says he enjoys the “sense of accomplishment”: “It’s a way I can be creative and actually be quite good at it.” There are other purported benefits to playing with Lego, such as improved mental health. Nick Bright runs Brighton Bricks, an adult Lego group that meets monthly, and says: “It’s therapy by stealth, you don’t even realise you’re helping your wellbeing.” Like many adult fans, the 51-year-old rediscovered Lego later in life. He recalls the product that revived the habit: “It was the Haunted House Monster Fighters set. It was one of those moments where you go ‘Yeah, this is me’.” He shares his love for Lego with his nine-year-old son and 80-year-old mother. His home collection is large and admits “my wife maybe thinks I have too much”. There are plenty of gateways into the hobby through collaborations with the likes of Disney, Dune and Fortnite, but Bright warns that one downside is that “there are a lot more bigger, expensive sets and there is a fear of missing out”. Bright prefers to follow the guide of a Lego set’s printed instructions, but has many friends whose constructions come from their own imagination.

events.title: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?
events.summary: Andy Burnham is in need of radical proposals. A ‘care first’ year in exchange for 50% off fees could be just what he needs T he UK’s social care sector is in crisis. Costs are spiralling, with many local councils forced to dedicate the vast majority of their budgets to it. At the same time, more and more families are seeing their savings disappear into the black hole of nursing home fees. With an ageing population, the problem is set to get worse. In only his second week as prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to succeed where so many of his predecessors have failed: by fixing Britain’s social care system. And yet, as parliament returns from recess, the new-ish administration is still worryingly unclear about how it will do this. Despite Burnham declaring that care workers should enjoy better compensation, we don’t know how he plans to pay for any of it – not least because he has kept Starmer’s campaign pledge to not raise income tax, VAT or national insurance. At the moment, it looks as though it will be impossible to square the circle. What the government needs is big, innovative ideas. We should look to history for inspiration, while also absorbing the lessons of past mistakes. How about national service – but instead of entering the military, recruits are pledged to the NHS? Eye-catching, but ultimately not right, at least not in that form. Forcing young people to do work they’d prefer not to, when there isn’t even an enemy at the gates, will only lead to bad results. Indeed, the army has already learned this: compulsory recruits in the postwar period were typically unmotivated and incompetent; a drag rather than a boost to the military’s performance. But that’s a crude precedent. We can take more relevant inspiration from elsewhere. For example, young men in Austria who do not wish to serve in the military can instead opt for health or social care work; many end up driving ambulances. The trade-off is that they do nine months instead of six. In Norway, conscientious objectors were, until 2012, able to perform “civilian national service”, working in community settings such as primary schools or nursing homes, and accruing points towards university entry for doing so. Thinking along similar lines, how about this? The government offers recent school leavers a deal: 50% off their total university fees if they first spend a year volunteering in social care. (You could even up the ante: 100% off if they commit to two years; full back pay with a bonus if they stay in the profession.) There are many reasons to take this proposal seriously. First, it is not just social care that is in crisis. University funding is, too. Right now, UK universities are panicking because student enrolment fees no longer keep them in the black. But at the same time, undergraduates are being presented with eye-watering loan bills and interest rates at levels that make capital repayment much harder. We are rapidly approaching a cliff edge. The government is going to have to fix the system one way or the other. Why not do something innovative and radical at the same time? The overall maths might work surprisingly well. If uptake is sufficiently high, the state gets an enormous amount of free (in the short term) labour to offset the costs of lost loan revenue. If that sounds exploitative, remember that it would be in the interests of young people themselves (in the longer term) because they would leave university with a heck of a lot less debt. But the upsides go beyond just money. At the moment, unscrupulous agencies too often rely on low-paid migrant labour, ignoring the linguistic and caring skills required do a safe and competent job. A scheme like this would open up a new pool for recruitment – of eager-to-learn young people at the start of their careers. Of course, they would have to undergo proper training and would only get the discount if they complete the programme to a certified high level. Along the way, some would discover that care work can be deeply rewarding; that the current stigmatisation of this kind of employment just doesn’t tally with reality. I know, because since I broke my neck in a rock-climbing accident in 2023, I have relied on 24-hour live-in care. I am lucky to be with a very good agency , which only employs highly competent and conscientious staff (from all over the world). I have seen up close just how rewarding and dignified care work can be. Sure, there are some icky parts to looking after a man who can’t go to the toilet by himself. But all my care workers take real pride in helping me live as close to a normal life as possible. Of course, they’re not on footballers’ wages. But they get a very visible amount of life satisfaction from helping me find mine. One of the most interesting care workers I’ve met was covering holiday earlier in the summer.

events.title: Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England? | John Harris
events.summary: Cities are the big winners in Burnham’s devolution drive. But what happens to the rest of England? Labour has promised a ‘fundamental rewiring’ of power. But some areas are years into their devolution journey while others scramble to get started A part from the joyous hyperactivity that comes with suddenly making it to No 10, there are good reasons why Andy Burnham seems to be a prime minister in a hurry. If he decides that his first term is going to run to its maximum length, he has three years, which is a maddening time-frame: too long for him to just tinker here and there, set out his long-term vision and then ask the electorate for permission to do more, but probably too short to start and finish many of his key projects. His chosen solution, it seems, is a mixture of the strategies he would use for each approach, which includes running at some issues at breakneck pace. So it is with his specialist subject: devolution for England. The huge changes now afoot actually began under Keir Starmer, with the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act passed earlier this year. Areas that previously had two tiers of local government will see them replaced with new unitary councils. But the most historic move centres on regional mayors – what the government calls “strategic authorities” – and a shift that the Whitehall PR machine is hyping up as a “fundamental rewiring of the way our country works, surrendering power that for too long has been held in Westminster and Whitehall”. In principle, this is unquestionably worth celebrating. But it also gives rise to a whole range of increasingly urgent and awkward questions. One change became clear earlier this year, and now looks like it will be turbocharged . By April 2027, regional and metro mayors will be able to keep as-yet-unspecified quantities of the business rates generated in their areas, and from the following year onwards, they will retain a share – also yet to be announced, presumably because the Treasury and No 10 North are wrestling with it – of local income tax receipts. These revenue streams will replace existing Whitehall grants rather than being additional money. But Burnham’s announcements have, among the more established and confident mayors, triggered visions of even greater liberation from Westminster and Whitehall, and possible command of schools, GP services, childcare and much more. There are also welcome predictions of loans being taken out against mayoral authorities’ projected income to fund long-overdue projects, most promisingly in housing and public transport. England’s 14 regional and metro mayors are right to see a growing opportunity for a civic political renaissance. Burnham and his people are equally correct in their conviction that improving public services and infrastructure, and firing up growth, demands a leading role for these mayors. But whatever the PM’s insistence that he intends to foster “good growth in every postcode”, the core of the vision is undeniably city-based. As the London School of Economics’ local government expert Tony Travers told me last week: “The whole idea of this version of economic change, which is very embedded, is that the only way to make the economies of city regions work is by letting the central part of the city develop fast, and hope that people will commute in and out to take advantage of it.” And at that point, we should pause for thought. I write this from Somerset, which sits just outside the West of England mayoral combined authority (containing Bristol, South Gloucestershire, and Bath and North East Somerset) and therefore has no regional leader, nor yet plays any part in a strategic authority. Together with its neighbouring county of Wiltshire, it contains the sort of places that almost no one talks about: towns ringed by countryside or on the coast – Melksham, Bridgwater, Calne, Minehead , Trowbridge – that have experienced serious decline, and have been denied a voice for far too long. Too many places, in fact, are now years behind parts of the country whose devolution journeys began a long time ago. The best thing to be by far is an established mayoral strategic authority – which, according to a House of Commons library briefing , qualify for the widest range of powers and integrated multi-year funding settlements, and include Greater London, Greater Manchester, the Liverpool city region, the West Midlands and such recently elevated territories as Cambridgeshire and Peterborough and the aforementioned West of England. A second tier is reserved for such “mayoral strategic authorities” as Tees Valley, Greater Lincolnshire – led by Reform UK’s Andrea Jenkyns – and Hull and East Yorkshire, which have to wait at least 18 months after their foundation to join the top rank, and have more restricted or ringfenced funding.

events.title: UK asks banks for feelgood stories about keeping out dirty money
events.summary: City firms tapped for case studies to try to convince global watchdog that London has cleaned up its act The government is asking bankers and lawyers to provide feelgood stories about how they blocked dirty money from entering the UK, as ministers try to prove the UK’s money-laundering controls are working. The Treasury’s call for evidence is meant to illustrate that the UK has upped its game when it comes to preventing financial crime, particularly since its last dismal assessment by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) global crime watchdog in 2018, which fuelled allegations that London had become a hub for “dirty money” . “To build the strongest possible picture of system-wide effectiveness,” the government call for evidence said , “we are looking for real-life examples with clear, demonstrable results that illustrate how the UK’s anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and sanctions frameworks operate effectively in practice.” The government is rushing to collect those examples before it submits its own evidence packet to the taskforce in October. The watchdog’s assessment team will then visit the UK for an on-the-ground review next summer. But the UK faces an uphill battle to prove the City has made substantial changes, and are staying alert to new threats including a surge in AI-fuelled investment fraud and the growing popularity of cryptocurrencies, which can help shield the source of transactions. Last year, the National Crime Agency estimated that £100bn is being laundered through or within the UK every single year, with City firms providing legal and financial services for fraudsters, human traffickers, the illegal drug trade and other types of organised crime. The UK’s national risk assessment on money laundering and terrorist financing has also classed the UK legal sector as “high risk” for every one of its assessments since 2017. “As the UK approaches its next FATF mutual evaluation in 2027, the pressure on its anti-money laundering (AML) regime is intensifying,” the rating agency Moody’s said in a report published earlier this year. “Billions are spent each year in the UK on supervision with hundreds of firms refused entry to the financial system following due diligence, yet an estimated £100bn is still laundered annually.” Moody’s added: “When FATF examiners arrive in the UK, they may ask how much of that risk is really being reduced by the UK’s controls, intelligence and enforcement, and how quickly.” The first phase of the next FATF review will allow the UK government to submit its own evidence, outlining how effectively the country handles and prevents money laundering and other financial crime. The Treasury is asking City firms to share any cases, from 2022 onward, showing how they dumped, or refused to take on, potentially high-risk clients. That is on top of cases where a company’s intervention later led to a state investigation or prosecution. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The government has also asked companies for any examples where they discovered red flags for financial crime in customer profiles, and how this ended up changing the types of clients the firm was willing to take on. A Treasury spokesperson said: “We take firm and coordinated action across government and industry to crack down on economic crime. We have introduced new strategies, enhanced enforcement capabilities and increased funding designed to disrupt those seeking to abuse the UK economy. “As you would expect, the government regularly engages with industry on this - and preparations for the FATF assessment in 2027 are no different.”

events.title: Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income
events.summary: Inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks. The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation. Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%. In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168. The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027. McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy . Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings. "XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott. McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks. Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy . The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%. Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%. The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations. Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets. Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks. Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy , an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%. Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East. "We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta. Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty. Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking.

events.title: Taco Bell to return to UAE after 14 years as Americana Restaurants plans Gulf expansion
events.summary: Taco Bell is set to return to the UAE after 14 years under a new agreement with Americana Restaurants, with plans to expand the US fast-food brand into other Gulf markets. Americana Restaurants has signed an exclusive development agreement with Taco Bell UK and Europe, a subsidiary of Yum! Brands, to relaunch the chain in the UAE before a phased expansion across the Gulf. Taco Bell is the coolest brand in its category, built for a generation that wants great flavour, great value and a little attitude Mohamed Alabbar, chairman of Americana Restaurants The deal marks Americana’s entry into the Mexican-inspired quick-service restaurant segment and builds on its decades-long relationship with Yum! Brands. Americana already operates KFC and Pizza Hut across several markets in the region. “Taco Bell is the coolest brand in its category, built for a generation that wants great flavour, great value and a little attitude,” Mohamed Alabbar, chairman of Americana Restaurants said in a statement on Sunday. “Dubai adopts what’s bold and tells the world about it. We will start here, get it right, and scale Taco Bell across the UAE and the GCC.” The companies have not announced an opening date or location for the first restaurant. Wasn't Taco Bell already here? The launch marks Taco Bell’s return to the Emirates after more than a decade. The chain first entered the UAE in 2008 but withdrew in 2012. Taco Bell has not publicly provided a detailed explanation for its exit. However, a 2025 case study by Ivey Publishing attributed the withdrawal to “strategic misalignments” and fierce competition from established restaurant brands. The study also found the UAE market has changed significantly since Taco Bell's departure, including growth in its expatriate population and increased consumption of Mexican cuisine. The arrival of Chipotle's Mexican Grill in Dubai and Abu Dhabi in 2024 could serve as an example. It is managed by Alshaya Group, the Kuwait-based international franchise retail operator which has brought The Cheesecake Factory, P.F. Chang's, Shake Shack, Starbucks and other major American brands to the Middle East. This time, Americana and Taco Bell are positioning the UAE as the starting point for a broader regional push. The companies cited the country's diverse population, vibrant food culture and appetite for new concepts as reasons for launching there before expanding into other Gulf markets. 'Live More' in the Middle East Taco Bell is one of the biggest Mexican-inspired fast-food chains in the US. Entrepreneur Glen Bell opened its first restaurant in Downey, California, in 1962. Its menu is known for American takes on Mexican-inspired dishes, including tacos, burritos, quesadillas and nachos, as well as products such as the Crunchwrap Supreme. Menu innovation and value have become important parts of its identity in the US, where the company has also built a strong following among younger consumers. It's Live Más, or Live More , tagline, established in 2012, represented the company's aim to shift from focusing purely on food to a food experience. Globally, Taco Bell has more than 9,000 restaurants, including more than 1,200 across about 40 markets outside the US. Taco Bell also has another connection to the UAE. Mubadala Capital, the Abu Dhabi-based asset manager, acquired K-MAC Enterprises, one of the largest Taco Bell franchisees in the US, in 2021. K-MAC currently operates more than 350 Taco Bell restaurants across 10 US states. “We're excited to continue our strong international momentum in the UAE, to connect with a new generation of fans," said Sean Tresvant, chief executive of Taco Bell. Taco Bell will join a large portfolio of international and regional restaurant brands operated by Americana across the Middle East, North Africa and Kazakhstan. The group’s brands include KFC, Pizza Hut, Hardee’s, Krispy Kreme, Peet’s Coffee, Wimpy, TGI Friday’s, Costa Coffee, Baskin-Robbins and Chicken Tikka. Its more recent additions include Greek premium coffee, nuts and chocolate concept carpo and Lebanese quick-service restaurant Malak Al Tawouk. Americana operates across 12 countries and describes itself as the region's largest out-of-home dining and QSR operator.

events.title: I downsized from a house to a small apartment. I got rid of a lot, but kept one sentimental item.
events.summary: The author went back and forth about keeping a Tupperware bowl from his childhood while downsizing. Courtesy of Jesse Gormley I recently moved from a single-family home to a small apartment. During the move, I had to sort through my possessions and decide what to keep and what to let go of. I realized I didn't need most of my stuff, though I did keep a Tupperware bowl from my childhood. Recently, after a major change in my personal life, I relocated from a single-family home to a 660-square-foot apartment. Transitions are hardly ever easy. Among all the uncertainty that comes with moving from a large living space to a smaller one is figuring out what to do with all your stuff. It's a weird predicament to be in, standing inside what is soon to be your former house, surrounded by possessions and knowing that not all of them can come with you. When I started packing things up, some decisions took all of two seconds. The television was coming with me. So were my clothes, kitchenware, and the handful of pieces of furniture that would actually fit in my new apartment . Easy. After that, though? That's when the real decisions get made. I made three piles to help me decide what to take with me I found myself standing in the middle of the room holding things that had somehow survived every move I'd ever made. Empty iPhone boxes? Straight into the trash. Old moto jacket? That one stayed in my hands for a long bit while I tried to decide whether I still liked it or just liked the version of myself who used to wear it. Before long, I'd created three piles: keep, donate, and one more — the one that kept growing, and growing, and growing. The pile of "indecidables." As a kid, we had a very old-school, oversize yellow Tupperware bowl that served primarily as our popcorn bowl, but my mom used it at Christmastime to store her cookies. When I tell you this bowl is big, I mean you had to carry it with both hands, even as an adult. And I certainly didn't need it. I also didn't have a place to store it. It was in and out of the toss pile more times than I care to mention. Decluttering during the move changed my relationship with possessions Downsizing is low-key grief. You don't realize the invisible burden your possessions have been until it's time to part ways with them. Every box you tape shut is a decision. Every trash bag, a choice. As I began settling into my new place, I figured I'd miss the stuff I couldn't keep. What really surprised me, though, was how quickly it all kind of faded from my consciousness. It made me wonder whether I'd been hanging onto all of it for all those years because I needed it, or because I hadn't bothered to stop to ask if I still did. The author realized the Tupperware bowl he'd kept didn't fit neatly into his cupboards. Courtesy of Jesse Gormley A few weeks after moving in, I needed my drill to put something together. After searching high and low for the thing, I came to the horrifying realization that somewhere along the way, during my downsizing , the drill had either been tossed or donated. I was pretty annoyed with myself at first, wondering what other important things hadn't made it to the new place. The weird thing is, other than the drill, I couldn't recall a single other item that I actually missed. I guess I'd thought of all my stuff as just that: one big collective item. When I tried to break that image down into individual possessions, I began to realize that maybe none of it was nearly as important as I'd always thought. Still, though, I did end up grabbing that oversize Tupperware bowl as I was leaving. The thing is, I can't really point to a single defining memory associated with it. It wasn't the bowl from my birthday party or the one my mom always mixed cookie dough in, or anything like that. It was simply...there. Filled with popcorn during movie nights . Filled with Christmas cookies every December. It had been part of the background of my life for so long that leaving it behind felt stranger than finding a place for it in my new apartment. However, I still don't know where to keep it. It doesn't fit comfortably in any cabinet, so it wanders from shelf to countertop to pantry. But every time I see it, I'm reminded that not every possession earns its place because it's useful. Some earn it simply because they've quietly been with us for the whole time. events.title: I manage 10+ agents at Cisco. It doesn't mean longer hours, but the work can feel more intense.
events.summary: Sergio Freitas said he manages 10 to 20 agents daily, which manage their own agents. Khanchit Khirisutchalual/Getty Images Sergio Freitas is a senior director of engineering at Cisco and oversees 10 to 20 agents daily. Now that agents are writing more code, it requires more review, Freitas said. While he's not putting in more hours, he said the work is faster-paced and can feel more intense. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Sergio Freitas, senior director of engineering at Cisco, based in Lisbon, Portugal. His identity and employment have been verified by Business Insider. This story has been edited for length and clarity. I started as a software engineer, became a manager, and currently work as a director of engineering at Cisco, with four teams based in Portugal. Sergio Freitas said that AI agents have changed the pace of work. Sergio Freitas Software engineering has always gone through changes. There are always new technologies you have to learn, like programming languages or frameworks. Now, it's the way engineers work that's changing rapidly, and in the last year, it's changed significantly . People have to adapt to that, and that can cause stress. The biggest change came after frontier models launched at the end of last year, like Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.5 . That's when AI really started to be embedded in our workflows, and we began delegating and working with agents to do software engineering. We were using AI before, but more for autocomplete and prompting. Agentic AI has changed our work Our work as software engineers has changed from crafting the code to be focused on architecture, design, managing workflows and agentic orchestration. Engineers are shifting from manual work to becoming system architects and workflow orchestrators, allowing them to solve larger, more complex architectural problems. The agents are like teammates and I manage 10 to 20 agents daily, which manage other agents. The number of agents they manage depends on the complexity of the task. The main orchestrator agent can spawn sub-agents to complete specific tasks. They're always running and they're aware of collaboration platform notifications, GitHub pull requests, and other integrations when given explicit permission. For example, based on the description of a ticket in Jira, which is our project management and issue-tracking tool, an agent creates the code, and then that has to be reviewed by the person who owns the agent. It then goes through a review process, where at least two engineers have to review the code. About four months ago, we moved into loop engineering , where, instead of the agent asking questions, it loops, or keeps working until it gets the final response. Sometimes, depending on what needs to be done, the agent can ask for authorization to connect to certain systems or perform certain operations. More and more, it's autonomous, but strict guardrails remain. I'm reviewing more work There's a lot of value in having AI work with engineers, but they need to be conscious about reviewing the code. Everything that gets delivered to production is the human's responsibility, not the agent's. I'm not working more hours, but there is an aspect of AI that brings, in many occasions, more work to the table because it can do more. Cisco focuses a lot on security. So there are a lot of security scans you need to run, and conversations with the legal team that need to happen. It's a faster-paced job As engineers adapt to this new way of working, some initial fatigue comes from the ability to do more. You have to shift your attention a lot, which slows you down if you're not completing tasks end-to-end. As engineers adapt to higher daily output and multi-threaded collaboration with agents, they need to build new mental habits around multitasking and asynchronous review, which is a different cognitive exercise from traditional coding. It's a wider scope. At the end of the day, you feel you were more focused, but not in the way when you're coding and have to be in the zone for extended periods. Crafting code was a skill that you built, and not many people had it. It kind of felt like a superpower of being able to create something from scratch and code it yourself. If you're really into the code-crafting piece, it's a big change that some engineers struggle with. At the end of the day, it felt lighter. Now with the management of agents, it's faster-paced. events.title: Micro dramas are weird, cheap, soap operas for your phone. And they're booming.
events.summary: CandyJar; Getty Images; BI Micro dramas should be easy to ignore: How big could the market be for low-budget soap operas, designed to be consumed in one-minute chunks? Pretty big, it turns out: Possibly $14 billion a year. Much of that comes from China, where micro dramas started. But US apps like CandyJar say they're seeing real growth. And TikTok is looming … What if you could watch short videos on your phone? What if you could pay people to watch those videos? I know, I know: I'm describing Quibi , the infamous app that flopped in 2020. But: I'm also describing micro dramas — low-budget movies cut into one-minute chunks. And those do seem to be working: Consumers may be spending as much as $14 billion on them this year. Most of that spending is happening in China, where the genre took off. But micro dramas are breaking through in the US , too: Mainstream video platforms like Peacock are adding them to the mix, and US-based companies like CandyJar say they're seeing very fast growth as well. It may be that micro dramas have limited appeal, and won't grow beyond their current audience — primarily women looking for quick diversions, via Harlequin-style romances. But even if micro dramas end there, they would still represent a real change in the way at least some Americans get, and pay for, entertainment. Ali Albazaz thinks they will become much bigger: He's the CEO of Inkitt , a startup that began as a platform for amateur writers, which is now morphing into a micro drama player. It's the company that owns CandyJar, and which has also launched Ironblood , a micro drama vendor aimed at dudes who are happy to watch AI-generated action/adventure tales. I think also think it's possible that micro dramas get truly big in the US. But it's also possible to imagine that when that happens, the industry will be dominated by TikTok and Meta's Reels. Those platforms are already the main way apps like CandyJar find their customers. So why not just keep the whole thing for themselves? And indeed, TikTok is trying out multiple ways to tackle micro dramas, including a free, ad-supported app , as well as a paid version . "The competition is ruthless," Albazaz acknowledges. "There is risk and threat from every side." Albazaz walked me through micro drama economics and audience in the most recent episode of my Channels podcast, which also included an industry overview from Hernan Lopez, who runs the Owl & Co . entertainment consultancy. You can hear both conversations in their entirety here . The following is an edited excerpt of my talk with Albazaz. Peter Kafka: There's no shortage of short-form entertainment out there. Reels and TikTok give it to me for free, and they tune it to what I want. What are micro dramas providing that isn't already there, and why do people pay to watch them? Ali Albazaz: The user-generated content that you get on TikTok and so on don't do serialized content. So you don't have full dramas being told. Micro dramas really taught us that you can chop the movie into 90-second-long episodes and then sell individual episodes or a subscription. What's your budget for these shows? It costs about $200,000 to do a physical production in Los Angeles at this point. You can go from $150,000 to $300,000. We tend to be at the higher end. Does the production value matter to consumers? A lot of the stuff I see seems to be … the polite word, I guess, is "inexpensive." It seems like people are quite comfortable with that. What is the urge to up the ante on your end? You're correct to say that the majority of micro dramas look [like] very low-quality. But we really have very high expectations from our team, and we really want to stand out that way. CandyJar, and most micro dramas, are aimed towards women. You also recently launched Ironblood — action/adventure aimed at men. With those shows, you really lean into the idea that you're making them with AI. Why is that important to disclose, and are you worried about AI pushback? AI is allowing us to create movies that would normally be predominantly-CGI based, very, very cheaply. You can't afford Marvel-level CGI, but you can do an AI version of it. That's right. We had so many great stories that are superhero and action-based, and previously it would cost us $200 million to go out and produce them. But some people who are using AI try to hide it, and if it comes out that they're using it, it's a scandal. You guys clearly don't think that's a problem. We don't want to lie, right? We want to be open and honest with our users. Do these adventure stories that you're telling on Ironblood have the same budget as the romances you're showing on CandyJar? No. They end up being significantly cheaper. We're talking $10,000 to $50,000. What's the future of your business? Figuring out other micro drama formats? Or trying to branch out into things like traditional TV shows and movies? We're building the operating system for storytellers, whether they want to create a bestselling book, audiobook, or movie. We want to have movies that you can watch in the cinema. We want to create theme parks at some point. The idea is to really help storytellers tell their stories in all possible formats. events.title: It's Warren Buffett's 96th birthday. His last year was one of the most transformational yet.
events.summary: Warren Buffett is Berkshire Hathaway's chairman and former CEO. Daniel Zuchnik/WireImage Warren Buffett celebrates his 96th birthday on Sunday. He's retired as CEO, bet big on Alphabet, and ramped up his giving over the past 12 months. Here are the highlights from the legendary investor's landmark year. Happy birthday, Mr. Buffett. Investing legend Warren Buffett turns 96 on Sunday, and the 12 months since his 95th birthday have been truly transformational, featuring a huge career move and a major new investment. He's also accelerated his charitable giving and dispensed plenty of his trademark wit and wisdom. Into the next chapter For his Thanksgiving message , Buffett penned a love letter to his hometown of Omaha, reflected on his good fortune, and thanked the many people who helped him throughout his life. Buffett, who has pledged to donate virtually all of his wealth to good causes, said he would speed up his giving as he wanted his children to be the ones who distribute his fortune. He also encouraged his followers to learn from their mistakes, choose good role models, live up to the obituaries they want for themselves, and care for others. "When you help someone in any of thousands of ways, you help the world," he wrote. "Kindness is costless but also priceless." Buffett retired as Berkshire Hathaway CEO at the end of December after six decades in charge. He remains chairman of the company, which he transformed from a failing textile mill into a $1 trillion juggernaut. Sharing life lessons Buffett shared several pieces of life advice during a CNBC interview aired in January but filmed in May 2025. The billionaire warned against getting into debt as it leaves people "underwater" and unable to escape. He urged parents to practice what they preach and set good examples for their kids: "If you want to have good children, be a good parent." Buffett also recommended people find jobs they love so much that the "paycheck is incidental to what you're doing." The bargain hunter also vented about high asset prices constraining him from deploying Berkshire's capital, which has caused its cash pile to balloon. He said he'd be "willing to spend $100 billion this afternoon," as he'd much rather have that money in a  quality business  than in cash. The past and the present Berkshire's  annual report  highlighted Buffett's remarkable track record: Berkshire stock rose by about 6,100,000% between 1965 and 2025, trouncing the S&P 500's roughly 46,100% return, including dividends, over the same period. It also showed the power of Buffett's stock picks . Berkshire's Apple stake was worth 10 times its cost base at the end of December. Coca-Cola was up 21-fold, American Express was up 45-fold, and Moody's was up 51-fold. In a March interview with CNBC, Buffett said his life hadn't changed much since retiring as CEO. He's still commuting to Berkshire's headquarters in downtown Omaha five days a week, and continuing to pick stocks and field calls about potential acquisitions, albeit with his successor Greg Abel having the final say. Warren Buffett is still picking stocks and going to the office. Nati Harnik/AP Buffett also sat for a surprise interview during Berkshire's annual shareholder meeting in May. He warned of a "gambling mood" in markets, describing it as a "church with a casino attached." He said it was "not an ideal environment" for deploying cash, so he and his team were having to "pick our spots." Buffett also cracked a few jokes, replying when asked whether he'd met the new managers of some of Berkshire's key holdings: "I haven't met the old managers." Still in the mix In his July letter about his philanthropy, Buffett said he hoped to distribute his entire Berkshire fortune, over $140 billion, to good causes by the end of 2034. Buffett also told CNBC at the time that he'd "read a great deal" about his friend Bill Gates' ties to Jeffrey Epstein, and that while it was a "distasteful" situation, everyone makes mistakes when judging people. In the same interview, Buffett said he made the surprising call to invest in Alphabet last summer. Berkshire built that stake from scratch to nearly $38 billion by the end of June, making Google's parent company the third-biggest position in its stock portfolio after Apple and American Express. If Buffett is still behind that bet — likely given his early involvement, the size of the wager, and his confirmation that he's still picking stocks as chairman — it could be his last big play . Weeks away from his 96th birthday, Buffett said he felt fortunate to be alive and healthy, and while he was "losing marbles," he'd "accumulated marbles for a longer time than I deserved, and that's just a matter of luck." events.title: OpenAI and Anthropic are battling Big Tech for talent. We asked workers who's winning them over — and who's not.
events.summary: Mike Kostersitz (left), Abhinav Bohra (center), and Sneja Shah (right) shared their dream employers and the companies they might pass on. Mike Kostersitz (left), Abhinav Bohra (center), and Sneja Shah (right) Tech companies are competing fiercely for workers who can help them win the AI race. We asked eight tech workers for their dream employers — and the companies they'd pass on. Some favored OpenAI or Anthropic, while others preferred Big Tech. While tech companies are pouring billions into AI infrastructure , they are also competing fiercely for AI talent — and the AI boom is reshaping the choices available to workers. Alongside established giants like Apple, Google, and Amazon, frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic now offer the chance to work at the edge of a technological shift, with potentially significant financial upside. Meanwhile, years of tech layoffs have made job security a bigger consideration for many workers. We asked eight tech workers about their dream employer, the Big Tech companies they're most and least interested in, and whether they've pursued jobs at OpenAI or Anthropic. (Their responses have been edited for length and clarity.) AI labs have come calling. I haven't pursued them. Abhinav Bohra says he'd choose Amazon, with NVIDIA as his runner-up. Abhinav Bohra Abhinav Bohra is a senior applied scientist at Amazon. He's in his 30s and lives in Seattle. Have you tried to land a job at an AI lab like OpenAI or Anthropic? A couple of recruiters for AI labs have reached out to me, including one at another Big Tech company. I took the calls but never pursued them. Labs hire people to make models smarter. I build recommendation engines, and a frontier lab has no real use for one yet: no catalog, no sellers, no shoppers to rank for. The day one of them runs an actual marketplace, people like me get very interested in them. We're not there yet. Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for? Amazon, which is boring, so here's the runner-up: NVIDIA. Recommendation at scale has become an inference cost problem. Running a big model once is cheap. Running it for every search and every shopper in real time is where the money goes. When your unit of progress is the millisecond, NVIDIA sits upstream of everything. Each company could be a good fit for someone in my field, but I also imagine they all have teams I'd love and teams I'd dread. I'd choose Anthropic for its values Mike Kostersitz says Anthropic would be his dream employer outside Nike. Mike Kostersitz Mike Kostersitz is a senior director, product management at Nike. He's in his early 60s and lives in Oregon. If you could work for any tech company, what would it be? If I had to look outside Nike, Anthropic would be my dream employer. The pull is real, and the company's stated values align more closely with my own than some other companies. I took note when earlier this year, Anthropic refused a Pentagon push to strip out restrictions on mass surveillance and autonomous weapons use, a stand their own CFO said could cost the company billions in revenue . That's the kind of "values over dollars" moment most companies only talk about. I don't expect that to hold forever. Once they IPO , the pull toward shareholder value will grow, and I'd expect other priorities to erode over time as a result. But I'd still pick Anthropic as my top choice. Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for? Apple, hands down, I love the products and what the culture represents. Least would be Amazon. I have a number of friends who are current or former Amazon employees on the tech side, and not one of them has ever seemed excited to go to work there or felt like they were making a difference, beyond the paycheck being strong. Business Insider is speaking with tech workers who've found themselves at a corporate crossroads — whether due to a layoff, resignation, job search, or shifting workplace expectations. Share your story by filling out this form . I haven't applied to OpenAI or Anthropic Meta's scale is part of its appeal in the competition for AI talent. Imen Ben Youssef / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images This tech worker is a software engineer at Meta. If you could work for any tech company, what would it be? Honestly, the answer might be where I already am: Meta. The frontier labs get the headlines, but hyperscalers like Meta and Google are doing the same caliber of work: not just core model training and fine-tuning but building the insane infrastructure needed to serve this to billions of users. One reason I haven't tried to land a job at an AI lab like OpenAI or Anthropic is that the labs are running on investor capital , while the hyperscalers fund their AI push from core businesses that already make enormous money. They have different risk profiles, and I've been happy with mine. Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for? Most: Setting Meta aside, Google is the obvious choice for me. It's one of the few companies doing everything in-house, from TPUs to frontier models to products. That full stack under one roof is appealing. Least: Probably Apple, and honestly that's about fit, not the company. They build incredible products and their engineering is world class, but their working model is very different from what I'm used to. Teams there tend to work on a focused slice under a lot of confidentiality, while my career so far has been end-to-end ownership, seeing a system from design through production and operations. I'd choose SpaceX over any Big Tech company or AI lab A tech lead (not pictured) in the insurance industry says SpaceX is his dream employer, Justin Sullivan/Getty Images This tech worker is a tech lead at a company in the insurance industry. He's in his early 40s and lives in Atlanta. If you could work for any tech company, what would it be? If I could work for any tech company tomorrow, I'd choose SpaceX. Few organizations on the planet operate with that level of ambition, engineering rigor, and mission clarity. Being part of a team pushing toward interplanetary travel would be an opportunity to contribute to something far bigger than any one company. Between Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and NVIDIA, which company would you most (or least) want to work for? NVIDIA is the company I would choose. events.title: I help people retire abroad. How to decide if it's the right move, and how to prepare.
events.summary: Federica Grazi said people are often attracted by lifestyles abroad, but don't always consider the finer details. Courtesy of Federica Grazi Retiring abroad requires more than choosing where to live. Federica Grazi, who helps retirees relocate, shared her advice for deciding whether to move and how to plan. She says trial stays and healthcare planning are vital before relocating. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Federica Grazi, 34, who is based in London. She is the founder of Mitos Relocation Solutions, an advisory firm that helps retirees move abroad. It has been edited for length and clarity. There's often a big gap between people who dream of retiring abroad and those who actually take the first step toward it. For many, hesitation gets in the way, and the idea of moving remains a dream. People are often drawn abroad by the lifestyle, but making a successful move means considering the full picture, like healthcare, aging, and the tax implications of residing in a new location. Here are the five things I recommend everyone do before they retire abroad. 1. Test-drive your potential new home Spend an extended trial period , say three months, in the place you're thinking of moving to. It's not about visiting for a week in July or August. Go in the offseason and try living like a local, thinking about what your everyday life would look like. Rent an apartment, speak with locals and expats, and join community Facebook groups. I've had clients for whom something as simple as getting medication from a pharmacy became an important test of whether they could see themselves living somewhere. 2. Turn the dream into a decision If you're unsure about retiring abroad, it doesn't have to be all or nothing. The key is not to let inertia take over and leave it as a dream, but to move from a question mark to a clear yes or no. In addition to spending a trial period in the country, you can do smaller things like speaking to others who have already moved to the destination to understand how it works in practice, or get advice from an expert who can give you a full rundown. They could even go on a scouting trip for you. Grazi said people should try to live like a local before moving to a new location. Courtesy of Federica Grazi 3. Don't rush If you decide to retire abroad and you're excited about it, don't rush the move. Changing residency is an important moment, so make a clear plan for what needs to happen before you leave. Think about whether you need a visa, housing, and even how you'll move your pet. You should also deal with things that aren't necessarily pleasant, like your will. 4. Think about taxes People often focus on the lifestyle abroad and think, "I love it here. I'll figure everything else out later." But that can lead to big tax mistakes, which need to be addressed before you move. If you only discover a problem after the tax year has ended, there might not be much you can do about it. 5. Take healthcare seriously Healthcare is something you want to be thinking about before you need it. How do you access it? How much will it cost? What might happen if you end up in the hospital? If you wait until something goes wrong, you could find yourself having to react and needing to navigate an unfamiliar healthcare system before you're fully integrated. Often, when people say they hated living abroad and moved back, it's because they didn't do enough research or preparation beforehand. Retirement abroad should be a period of joy and expansion. Doing the planning beforehand means that once you arrive, you can actually enjoy it. Read the original article on Business Insider
